activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Gottfried Leibniz and is still standard in mathematics today.
story:
The letter was in the drawer with the seed packets, under a rubber band gone brittle. Raphael had opened the drawer looking for graph paper, because his grandmother's house had everything except what a person actually came for, and had found instead an envelope addressed to her in a looping hand, postmarked years before he was born. He did not read it. He set it on the table beside his textbook and spread out the problem Mr. Le had assigned, the one that had followed him here for the long weekend: a rectangle of garden against the shed, forty meters of fence for the other three sides, find the dimensions that give the greatest area.

His grandmother was at the sink washing lettuce that had already been washed. "You're doing homework at my table," she said, not as a complaint. "Your grandfather used to do that. He'd spread his papers out like he was invading somebody."

"He did homework? He was a machinist."

"He was a machinist who read. Don't ask me what." She flicked water off the lettuce. "The boreal wind comes off that field behind the shed, so if you're figuring where a garden goes, that matters more than you'd think."

He wrote the area as x times forty minus two x, because the side parallel to the shed needed fencing but the shed itself didn't, and for a while he just looked at it. The textbook wanted the derivative, and the textbook wrote the derivative as a fraction, dy over dx, which he had accepted all year without questioning, the way he accepted the cafeteria's Tuesday fish. Then his phone lit up on the table. Kaitlyn, from the group chat with Mederic in it.

ok serious question. why does the book write the derivative as a fraction when it's not one? mr le just says "notation." that's not an answer.

Raphael typed and deleted twice. He remembered Mederic proselytizing about some YouTube channel that treated every unresolved question as a personal insult, and how Raphael had envied the certainty. He typed: i looked it up once. it comes from leibniz and it's still standard in math today. so we're all just living in his handwriting. Kaitlyn replied with a single exclamation point, and Mederic sent, so it IS a fraction? and Raphael wrote no, and left it there, because that was the honest edge of what he knew.

He brought the exponent down, two x times forty minus two x became eighty x minus four x squared in the derivative, and he set eighty minus eight x equal to zero and got x equals ten. Ten meters out from the shed, twenty along it, a hundred square meters. He checked it by trying nine and eleven, both smaller, like the hill cresting exactly where he'd said it did. The notation was still bothering him, though, the fraction that wasn't a fraction, a thing that behaved in calculations as if it were something it wasn't. He thought about how much of what he trusted worked that way, and then stopped thinking about it, because his grandmother was drying her hands.

"So where's my garden?" she said.

"Ten meters out from the shed, twenty along. That's the biggest it can be with forty meters of fence. It's the maximum."

She came and looked at his page, at the parabola he'd sketched opening downward with its crown at ten. She put one finger on the drawing. "And this is certain?"

"As certain as math gets."

"Hm." She went back to the drawer, took out the envelope, and handed it to him. "You might as well. He wrote it to me before you existed and I've read it a hundred times. It's about the shed."

The letter was from his grandfather, written when the shed was new. It went on about the machine shop, the throughput of parts through his station, how many a shift, how the numbers had begun to feel like the only honest language he had. And then, near the end: the strip along the shed was the best ground on the property, and he had measured it with a tape, ten meters out and twenty along, before deciding against planting it, because he'd calculated that the hours of upkeep exceeded the yield. "The maximum is not always the thing you want," the letter said. "Sometimes the best ground is the ground you leave alone."

Raphael read it twice. His grandfather had done arithmetic, not calculus, and had arrived at the same rectangle by walking it with a tape measure, then walked away from it. Raphael had found the crest of the hill with a three-hundred-year-old notation and felt, for a moment, that he'd discovered something. He set the letter beside his textbook and looked at the two answers lying next to each other, the same and not the same.

"So do I fence it or not?" his grandmother said. She was smiling at the envelope, not at him.

"Your call. The math says a hundred square meters. He says leave it alone."

She folded the lettuce into a towel and carried it to the counter. "Then I'll tell you what I decided this morning, before you opened a single book." She opened the back door and nodded toward the shed. "I called the concrete man. That strip's becoming a patio."

Raphael looked out at the patch of ground he had optimized, already given over to lawn chairs in her mind, and began gathering his papers. "You could still put planters on the patio," he said, and she laughed and told him to close the screen before the mosquitoes came in.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
story:
The email from the new manager arrived at 4:52 on a Tuesday, while Benjamin was still at school, so he found it at home with his backpack half unzipped and his screen already awake. It outlined his summer schedule at the marina office: shifts, dress code, a reminder that the newsletter went out Fridays. It ended with a question about whether he could start Monday. Benjamin read it twice, and then, because the whole thing had the stiffness of someone trying very hard to sound professional, he typed back a reply he thought was obviously joking. "Monday works, though I should warn you I'm a committed hedonist and may demand breaks to watch the pelagic birds off the point." He signed it "Benjamin, Chief Seagull Correspondent" and hit send before he could second-guess himself.

He told Ewan about it the next morning, in the parking lot before first period. Ewan was applying to a summer research program and had his own emails to worry about, the kind with the word "sincerely" in them. "You wrote what to your manager?" Ewan said, laughing but also not laughing. "You've never met this person."

"That's the point," Benjamin said. "It's an icebreaker."

"She doesn't know it's an icebreaker."

Benjamin waved this away, and the day went on: a quiz in Ms. Sadeghi's class, lunch, a substitute for the last period. But at four o'clock he was home again, and the reply was sitting in his inbox with a subject line that just said "Re: Monday."

It was three sentences. The first stated that the office maintained a professional standard in all correspondence. The second asked whether there was "any concern about your commitment to this role." The third said a call would be arranged before Friday. There was no name at the bottom, only a signature block, and Benjamin sat looking at it for a long moment, his hand resting on the mouse without moving it, the cursor blinking in the search bar where he had already begun typing something.

What he typed was "email sarcasm readers study." He wasn't sure why, except that Ms. Sadeghi had mentioned something once, in passing, during a unit on communication, and the phrase had coagulated in his memory out of half a dozen things she'd said. The search returned a study from 2005 by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues, which had found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness. He read the summary twice, then clicked through to the page itself. The finding held for both directions of error, but what he kept circling back to was the writer's side: people were confident, the study said, and wrong about that confidence.

He called Ewan, who was at his own computer, revising his research application for the third time.

"I found that thing," Benjamin said. "The email study Ms. Sadeghi mentioned. Kruger and Epley, 2005. Email writers overestimate how well readers pick up their intended tone, like sarcasm versus seriousness."

"I told you," Ewan said. "I told you yesterday."

"You laughed at the seagull thing."

"I laughed and told you. Both can be true." There was a pause, and the sound of Ewan typing on his end. "Look, my thing is due at midnight and I've cut four paragraphs and I can't tell if it's better or just shorter. Can we do this fast?"

Benjamin said they could, and hung up, and opened a new message. He sat with his fingers on the keys. The old impulse was to send something else funny, something that would prove the first one had been a joke, which he now understood would be exactly the same mistake wearing a different hat. The opposite impulse was to apologize so thoroughly that he'd sound like someone with something to apologize for, which was also not true. What he actually believed, he decided, was complicated: the joke had been a reasonable thing to want to say, and a bad thing to send, and he didn't think those two facts canceled each other out. What he couldn't tell, sitting there, was whether the manager was genuinely annoyed or was herself performing a professional standard in the same way he had been performing irreverence, two people typing at masks. The study said nothing about that part.

He wrote four drafts. In the first he kept the joke and explained it, which read like pleading. In the second he removed all personality, which read like a lawyer's letter. The third began "I want to clarify my previous email," which he liked until he read it aloud. The fourth was shorter. "Thank you for the schedule," it began. "My earlier email was meant as a joke, and I can see now that it didn't land as one; that was my mistake in judgment about tone, not a reflection of how I'll approach the job. I'm glad to start Monday and glad to talk by phone beforehand if that's useful." He read it once more, changed "glad" the second time to "willing," changed it back, and sent it before five.

Then he sat with the sent message open, doing nothing, while outside the light went long and orange across the neighbor's roof. Ewan texted a thumbs-up and a line about his application being done, one way or another. Benjamin's inbox refreshed once, twice, an advertisement arriving, nothing else.

At 6:40 the phone rang, a number with the marina's area code. He looked at it for two full rings before picking up.

"Benjamin? It's your manager. Before anything else," she said, "tell me about the seagulls."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Signalling before a merge or lane change warns other drivers of the move; signalling too late, or not at all, gives them no time to adjust.
story:
The cones were set up along the curb outside his grandfather's house, two garbage bins standing in for the parked cars, and Jason had been failing at the gap between them for most of Saturday morning. His grandfather sat in the passenger seat with his coffee going cold in his lap, saying nothing after the fourth attempt, which was worse than the shouting Jason had been half expecting.

"You're oversteering," his grandfather said finally. "You turn the wheel like it insulted you."

Jason pulled forward again, reversed, watched the bin in the mirror slide closer, and stopped with the rear tire a hand's width from the curb. Not perfect, but in. He sat with his hands on the wheel and let out a breath.

"All right," his grandfather said. "Now the road."

The test was in eleven days. Frederick had passed his own the month before and had texted a long account of everything the examiner had flagged, the most serious being the merge onto the highway, which Frederick described as "the part where they decide if they hate you." Jason had read the manual twice; he was, by habit, something of an autodidact, and he had memorized the sequences, the mirror order, the speed for the ramp. But the manual was words, and the ramp was a shrinking lane with real cars in it.

His grandfather drove them out to the loop of highway that circled the far side of town, the old two-lane section where the on-ramp was long and the traffic was thin on a Saturday. They switched seats. "Get up to speed before the end of the ramp," his grandfather said. "Don't make them slow down for you."

The first merge went badly in a way Jason hadn't anticipated. He checked the mirror, found a pickup truck two lanes' distance back, and flicked the signal on at the same instant he began moving the wheel. The truck's horn sounded before he was halfway into the lane, and he yanked the car back, heart hammering, the tires shuddering on the ridged shoulder.

"He had nowhere to go," his grandfather said. He wasn't shouting. He said it the way he said most things, as though stating a fact about weather. "You put the signal on when you were already moving. Give them the blinker early. Otherwise it doesn't tell them anything they don't already know."

Jason wanted to argue that the truck had been far enough back, that there had been space, but he knew it was the kind of thing a petulant child says when the fault is his, so he said nothing and drove the loop again. On the second pass he signalled a full three seconds before he began to move. The sedan behind him in the right lane eased off slightly, and its driver lifted two fingers off the wheel, which Jason understood was not a insult for once but a small acknowledgment, and he slid into the lane with room to spare.

They did it six more times, and by the fifth it had stopped feeling like a procedure and started feeling like a sentence in a conversation he was only now learning to speak. The signal wasn't for him; it was for the other driver, and it only worked if it arrived early enough to be answered. He thought of Frederick's text, of the manual's dry phrasing, and understood that the manual had been telling the truth but not the whole truth, that the whole truth included the horn and the two lifted fingers and the way a stranger eased off the accelerator for you because you had warned him you were coming.

At the house that evening, Yohan came by with his own learner's permit and a story about failing the written test twice, and the three of them, grandfather and two boys, sat on the porch while the grandfather let Jason explain the merge. Jason caught himself wanting to prevaricate about the horn, to soften the first failed attempt into something tidier, and instead he told it straight, the signal too late, the truck, the shoulder. Yohan asked whether three seconds was a rule or a guess, and Jason said he didn't actually know where the line was, only that there was a line, and that on one side of it strangers adjusted for you and on the other side they honked.

His grandfather stood, gathered the empty glasses, and paused at the door. "Tomorrow we do the bins again, then the ramp. And this time you signal for the parking too, even though there's nobody there." He went inside. Jason and Yohan sat in the fading light, and Yohan said, "He does that too? Mine just yells." Jason looked down the street at the curb where the bins still stood, the gap between them still there, waiting for morning.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and old paint, and Austin stood at the center of it with a clipboard he had borrowed from the library and a copy of the one-act tucked under his arm. Mr. Robinson had given him the slot for the spring showcase, told him the stage was his for two weeks of rehearsals, and then left him entirely alone with six actors who were mostly older than he was. That first afternoon he spread his blocking notes across the floor with blue tape, little arrows that looked, from the balcony, like a diagram of something circulatory.

Ella played the daughter, and she was the only one who took him seriously from the start. "Where do you want me at the top of the scene?" she asked, script rolled in one hand, and Austin consulted his notes and said, kitchen, downstage, and she walked there without complaint. The others drifted, checked their phones, laughed at things behind him that he could not see. He wondered whether authority was something you had before you directed or something directing gave you, and whether anyone in the history of theater had figured out the order.

The trouble came on Tuesday, and it came in a single word. He wanted the father figure, played by a tall junior, to cross toward the window during the long speech about the car accident, so Austin called out, "Move left." The junior moved left. The junior moved to the audience's left, which was to Austin's right, and collided with the chair that marked the kitchen table, and Meganne, who had been leaning on it, nearly went down. Everyone froze. Austin's face went hot, and he heard himself say, "No, the other left," which made it worse, because the junior just stood there between the tape arrows with his arms out.

"You said left," the junior said.

"I know. I meant my left." Austin turned to face the empty bleachers, the audience that wasn't there yet, and then turned back, and something rearranged itself behind his eyes. "Wait. It's not my left either. It's yours." He walked to the junior's mark and stood where the actor would stand, looking out at the bleachers. His left hand was on the side the audience would call right. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience." He said it mostly to himself, testing it, and then louder. "So they're backwards from what the audience sees. From now on I'll say stage left or stage right, and we'll both know."

Ella grinned at him from the kitchen. Meganne said, nonchalant, not looking up from her script, "Took you long enough," but she said it warm, the way you tease someone you've decided to keep. Austin marked the correction in his notes, crossed out "move left" and wrote "cross stage right," and thought about how many other things in the world might be named from a position he wasn't standing in. His mother spoke about money from where she stood. His ex-friend spoke about the fight from where he stood. He didn't finish the thought out loud.

The subpoena arrived on Thursday, not for Austin but for Mr. Robinson, who had been named in some dispute over the district's budget for the arts, and for two days the rehearsal space felt provisional, as though the showcase itself might be called into question by a court. Austin photocopied his script at the corner store before school and hand-delivered copies, and Meganne told him he was treating a one-act about a kitchen argument like it was a subpoenaed document, and he said maybe good work deserved the same care either way. She didn't laugh, exactly. She looked at him a half second longer than usual.

By Friday he had learned to give notes the way a stage manager would, specific and positional and calm, and the junior, whose name was also the name of a brand of soap and who had forgiven him entirely, crossed stage right on cue during the accident speech and it worked, the movement worked, it burnished the speech somehow, gave it a direction and a weight it had not had read sitting down. Ella watched the cross and then delivered her next line to the window instead of to the door, changing Austin's blocking without asking, and he opened his mouth to object and then closed it, because her choice was better. The scene had begun to belong to them.

He still didn't know if he was a director or just a seventeen-year-old with tape and a clipboard, and he suspected the two might not be different things, or might be different in a way nobody would ever tell him. On the last day of the first week he stood alone on the empty stage after everyone had gone, facing the bleachers, lifting first one hand and then the other, saying quietly, "Stage left. Stage right." The gym doors banged open down the hall, and Ella's voice came from somewhere near the lockers: "Austin, are you talking to yourself in there?"

"Come block your window scene," he called back.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
The chocolate had failed twice, and Owen had brought both failures with him in a paper bag, which now sat on the steel counter between him and the evidence. He unwrapped the first bar, the one he'd made in his own kitchen on Sunday, and tilted it toward the window where the last of the afternoon light came through the steam. It was dull as an old coin, and when he snapped a corner off, it bent first, then crumbled, then melted against his fingers without ever breaking clean.

"You brought your failures to work?" Abbey said. She was stacking clean ramekins at the other end of the pastry station, close enough to watch but not close enough to be asked to help, which was how she preferred most things.

"I brought my evidence." Owen dug the second bar out of the bag and set it beside the first. Same recipe, same moulds, same week. "This one I cooled in the fridge. This one I left on the counter overnight. Both of them came out like this."

Ms. Sutherland, the owner and, on Saturdays, the only person who outranked the dishwasher, was taciturn by reputation and by practice, and she said nothing for a while. She picked up the fridge bar, turned it over, pressed her thumb into a bloom of grey streaks along its surface, and set it back down. Then she walked to the dry storage shelf, exhumed from behind the flour sacks a battered plastic binder that Owen had never seen before, and dropped it on the counter in front of him.

"Read the section on cocoa butter," she said. "Then we'll do it on the slab."

Talia came through the kitchen door still in her coat, carrying a bag of tangerines she'd apparently decided someone needed. She peeled one, perched on a stool near the walk-in, and watched over Owen's shoulder while he read. The binder said what his phone had said three nights ago, in almost the same words, but reading it here, with the failed bars sitting there like patients, made it land differently. Cocoa butter could crystallize in six different forms, the page said, and only one of them was worth having. Tempering aimed to make most of the cocoa butter set in form V, the crystal form that gave shine and snap. Everything else was a lesser arrangement, dull, soft, unwilling to break.

"Six forms," Talia said, licking tangerine off her thumb. "So you rolled a one, basically. Twice."

"Something like that." Owen turned the page. There was a diagram of temperatures going up, then down, then held, and he copied the numbers onto his forearm with a pen because the notebook he'd brought was in his other jacket.

Ms. Sutherland came back with a bowl of dark callets and set a saucepan of water on low. "Melt it to forty-five," she said. "Stir. Don't let the bowl touch the water, and don't leave it, because if you burn it, none of the rest matters." She said this the way she said everything, flat and unhurried, and then she stood beside him with her arms crossed, which Owen understood to mean she was teaching without performing the part of a teacher.

While the chocolate melted, Abbey wandered over and began reading the binder upside down. "It's like the chocolate has six different personalities," she said, "and you have to talk it out of all but one of them."

"That's not what it says."

"I'm paraphrasing. Ms. Sutherland, am I allowed to paraphrase?"

"You're allowed to wash that bowl when he's finished with it."

Abbey smiled and went back to her ramekins, and Owen felt the small ridiculous pull to defend Abbey's paraphrase, or maybe Abbey herself, from nothing in particular. There was a boy in his chemistry class who flattered the teacher so constantly that Talia called him a sycophant with a name attached, and Owen had laughed at the time, and still laughed, but he noticed that Abbey's chatter in this kitchen did something like the opposite of that: it made the room easier rather than smaller. He filed the thought away and went back to stirring.

At forty-five degrees he poured two thirds of the chocolate onto the cold marble slab and worked it with a scraper and a palette knife, spreading it thin and gathering it back, spreading and gathering, while Ms. Sutherland watched the pool with the thermometer. The chocolate thickened, went matte, began to feel like it was deciding something. "Twenty-eight," she said. "Now back into the bowl." He scraped it in and stirred, and the bowl came up to thirty-one and held, glossy and even, and Ms. Sutherland dipped the tip of a knife and waited. The chocolate on the knife set in under a minute, hard and smooth, without streaks.

"Form V," Owen said, mostly to himself. "Most of it, anyway."

"Most of it," Ms. Sutherland agreed. She nodded at the moulds he'd brought, the same ones that had produced his two failures. "Pour."

He poured a thin, even stream into each cavity and tapped the mould flat against the counter to lift the bubbles out, and then they all stood there, four people and a tray, watching chocolate become something in the cool of the kitchen. Talia offered around the last tangerine. Abbey washed the bowl without being told, water running loud in the sudden quiet.

After ten minutes Owen turned the mould over and tapped it, and the bar dropped into his palm, shining under the fluorescent light like wet river stone. He took the corner between his fingers and broke it, and the crack went through the whole bar clean and sharp, a sound like a small door closing.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: The Framingham Heart Study, which began following residents of Framingham, Massachusetts in 1948, gave medicine the term 'risk factor' for habits and conditions that raise later disease risk.
story:
Annabelle had been sitting in Ms. Iyer's classroom for eleven minutes and had not yet said the true reason she was there. The mentorship meetings were supposed to be about college applications, and Ms. Iyer had her file open, pen resting on the transcript like a conductor's baton, waiting. Outside, the January light had the dull silver of a screen left too long on one image.

"Your essay draft," Ms. Iyer said. "You told me Thursday you'd bring it."

"It's on my laptop. It's not finished." Annabelle opened the computer anyway, more to have something to do with her hands than to show anything. On the screen behind the half-blank document was a message from her mother, sent at 6:14 that morning: They're keeping her another night. They want to talk to her about her habits. Habits, as though her grandmother were a child caught biting her nails.

"Annabelle."

"I'm deciding between two schools." It came out flat, a rehearsal of what she'd prepared. "The one near home, and the one in Montreal."

"Both good programs?"

"The near one is better for what I say I want. Probably." She turned the laptop toward Ms. Iyer so the essay, three paragraphs of careful nothing, would face her instead. Ms. Iyer read slowly, which Annabelle had learned was not hesitation but method, and the radiator ticked under the window like something counting.

At the hospital two nights earlier, her grandmother had been propped against pillows with the rail up, looking smaller than she had ever looked, and a young doctor had come in with a clipboard and asked, one by one, questions that seemed to have nothing to do with her heart. Did she smoke, ever. How much, how long. What she drank, how she slept, who she lived near. Her grandmother answered each one plainly, and when Annabelle asked afterward why they cared about all of it, why not just the heart, her grandmother had been matter-of-fact, almost cheerful, the way she was when she knew something Annabelle didn't.

"Because of Framingham," she had said. "There was a study, in a town in Massachusetts, they started following everyone there in 1948. That's where doctors got the term risk factor."

"From a whole town?"

"A whole town, for decades. So now they ask about your habits instead of waiting." She had folded her hands on the blanket. "Every answer I give them, I'm giving them a fact about 1994, or 1971. That's the strange part. They're asking a sixty-year-old me questions to learn about the me sitting here."

Annabelle had written none of this down, and yet here it sat in her chest during the mentorship meeting, heavy and specific, while Ms. Iyer was asking whether the essay's third paragraph could be more concrete. Ms. Iyer had a way of waiting that made silences go ductile, bendable, and Annabelle felt herself being shaped by it, bending toward the thing she had not said. She thought of Jasleen, who had chosen her school in one afternoon, and of Linkin, who had made a spreadsheet with weights and probabilities, who called Annabelle's indecision "being a dissident against your own data." He meant it as a joke. It hadn't entirely assuaged her, then or now.

"The essay's not the problem," Annabelle heard herself say. "The problem is I don't know what I'm deciding. I keep thinking it's about programs, or distance, or money. And then I think it's actually about one thing that won't happen for years."

Ms. Iyer set the pen down. "What thing?"

Here was the part she had been circling. "My grandmother's in the hospital. She'll be fine, probably. But sitting there, the doctor asked her all these questions about her past, and she said the answers were like... information she'd been mailing forward for decades, and it just arrived." Annabelle's voice stayed even, which surprised her. "So if I pick the far school, or the near one, I'm mailing something forward too. I just can't read it yet. And everyone keeps asking me to read it now, today, so I can pick."

For a moment Ms. Iyer looked at her the way the doctor had looked at the clipboard, as if the answer needed to be taken down exactly. "When is your grandmother coming home?"

"Maybe tomorrow. Maybe Friday."

"Then the essay can wait until Monday." She closed the file folder and slid it aside, making room on the desk for nothing, a cleared space. "Go see her after school. Bring the laptop if you want, but don't show her the essay."

"What would I show her?"

"The two schools. She got a whole town's worth of questions from one doctor. I suspect she'd be good at this."

Annabelle laughed, a short sound she hadn't expected, and began closing the laptop, then stopped with it half shut, the screen's light narrowing to a bright line on her fingers. On the way to the hospital she would stop and buy the ginger candies her grandmother pretended not to want, and she would ask her, over the rail of the bed, which of the two she would have chosen at seventeen, and whether the answer had arrived yet.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The kitchen smelled of burnt garlic, and Mikael's mother had surrendered the room to the three of them around eleven, saying only, "Don't set off the smoke alarm again." Eve had commandeered the good chair by the window, spinning her phone in her hand while Mikael scrolled with his elbows on the counter. Arianna sat on a stool between them, unfinished summer reading splayed and ignored on her knees, because Mikael had just held up his screen and said, "You have to see this."

The video showed a flooded street, brown water to the door handles of parked cars, a man carrying a dog above his waist. The caption said it was from that morning, from the city two hours south of theirs, and that two more dams were expected to fail by nightfall. Mikael's thumb hovered over the share arrow. "My aunt lives down there," he said. "I should send it to her so she knows."

"Don't," Arianna said, before she had fully decided to say it.

He looked up. Eve looked up. "It's flooding somewhere," Arianna went on, more carefully now, "but I saw something like this last month that turned out to be from years ago. Everyone passed it around like it was happening that day, including me. I reposted a wildfire clip that was four years old and felt like an idiot." She took a drink of her Coke, buying a second. "There's this thing a librarian showed us senior year. SIFT. It's from an educator named Mike Caulfield. Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context."

"Trace them to what?" Eve asked.

"The original context. Like where the clip actually started." Arianna pulled her phone out. "So, stop first. Don't share it yet."

Mikael lowered his phone with theatrical reluctance, and Eve dragged her chair closer, which was Eve's way of apologizing for the eye-roll she'd started and abandoned. Arianna took a screenshot of a distinctive frame, the man and the dog against a storefront with a green awning, and dropped it into a reverse image search. The loading wheel spun while the burnt-garbage smell thickened and Mikael cracked a window without being asked, which she noticed, and which she would remember later as the small, unannounced kindness it was.

The results came back in a scatter of thumbnails. The same man, the same dog, the same green awning, dated three years earlier, on a local news site covering a hurricane in an entirely different state. Eve read over her shoulder and said, quietly, "So the flood's real, just not this flood." Arianna scrolled further and found one aggregator that had stripped the date entirely, and beneath it a comment thread full of people in the southern city posting anxiously about their own streets, dry streets, asking whether they should evacuate. The video had become a kind of invasive species in the information biome, Arianna thought, spreading faster than anything that checked it, her own repost from June a vestigial appendage of that same machine, a share button pressed and never used again.

"Okay," Mikael said. "I won't send it. But my aunt's still down there, and if it is flooding, she should know." That was the part Arianna had been turning over without naming it: stopping wasn't the same as knowing. She ran a search for the city plus the word flood plus the current date, and found the county emergency page, updated that morning, reporting a burst storm main in one neighborhood and nothing about dams. She texted Mikael the link, and he forwarded it to his aunt with a note she couldn't see, his thumb moving fast now.

Then her own phone buzzed. A notification from her cousin: Arianna, is that flood video you posted real? My roommate's packing her car. Arianna stared at it. The wildfire clip she'd reshared in June had been harmless, old and far away, but somewhere in her contact list it had apparently lived on, been reshared and recontextualized until it had washed back up in her own family, wearing today's date. She typed, deleted, typed again. It's not from this week. I checked. I'll show you how when you're home.

Eve was watching her face. "What?"

"Someone I sent that wildfire thing to in June is asking about a flood video." Arianna laughed once, not because it was funny. "It got to my cousin's roommate before I could take it back."

"That's the twist," Mikael said, popping the tab on a soda he'd somehow located behind the bread box. "You were the source someone should have investigated."

Arianna put her phone face down on the counter, then picked it back up and opened her cousin's thread again, thumb hovering over the send arrow, checking the message twice before she let it go.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: JUnit's assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second, so swapping them gives confusing failure messages.
story:
The laptop sat open on his grandfather's kitchen table, between a bowl of walnuts and a crossword folded to the cryptic page. Owen had come here to work because the house was quiet in a way his own was not, and because his grandfather, who had spent forty years in banking, understood that some afternoons were for labour. Ms. Chowdhury had assigned it for Monday: a BankAccount class in Java, private fields, getter methods, a JUnit test for each one. Owen had never built a class before. He had written loops and if-statements, little machines that did one thing and dissolved, but this was different. A class stayed. It sat in the file like something with a body.

He typed the fields first, the way she had shown on the board: private double balance; private String owner;. The word private felt strange at first, almost secretive, but he was beginning to see it as the opposite. Privacy here meant the balance could not be touched from the street. It could only be asked about, politely, through a getter, a method that reported the number without letting anyone rewrite it. His grandfather, shelling walnuts across the table, glanced at the screen. "Encapsulation," Owen said, mostly to himself. "Like a fiduciary. The class holds the money for someone else, and it can't just spend it." His grandfather nodded slowly, as if this were the first sensible thing a young person had said to him all week.

Remi arrived at four with his own laptop and a bag of apricots from the tree in his yard. They spread out on the porch instead, the two of them, because the afternoon had turned golden and the wireless reached the wicker chairs. Nikolai joined by call, his voice tinny from the phone propped against a pitcher of lemonade. They each had to submit their own classes but they were allowed to compare tests, and Remi had already written his. "Mine's failing," Remi said, tipping the screen toward Owen. "Look. It says expected 50.0 but was 0.0, and I set the balance to fifty in the setup. How is it zero?"

Owen leaned over. The failure message sat at the top of the red bar like a verdict, and Remi kept rereading it as if it might soften. Owen read the line of the test itself. assertEquals(account.getBalance(), 50.0). The getter first, the number second. "Wait," Owen said. He scrolled up to his own test on his laptop, where he had written the arguments the other way around, the number first, the call second. His test passed. He looked between the two screens. "I think it's the order. I think assertEquals takes the expected value first and the actual value second."

"Which means what?" Nikolai asked through the phone.

"Which means your test expected zero and got fifty. You didn't fail because the balance was wrong. You failed because you told the test the wrong thing to expect." Owen said it carefully, testing the sentence as he spoke it. Remi stared at the message again, and Owen watched the confusion rearrange itself on his face, the moment when expected 50.0 but was 0.0 flipped inside out and became, in truth, expected 0.0 but was 50.0. Remi swapped the two arguments, ran the test, and the bar went green. He exhaled the way people do after a long held breath.

They worked until the porch shadows stretched across the boards. Owen finished his getters, then a deposit method for extra credit, then the tests, watching each bar fill green one at a time. Nikolai argued over the phone that getters were a waste of time, that if you wanted the balance you should just make the field public and read it, and Owen found himself disagreeing before he had fully thought it through. He understood the appeal; the getter seemed like a locked door beside an open window. But the locked door was the point. The class made a promise about what could change and what could only be asked, and the promise was worth the small ceremony of the asking. Still, he conceded, he wasn't certain where the line fell. Maybe some fields deserved to be public. Maybe the whole discipline was a habit you learned before you knew which parts of it mattered.

"Grandpa," he called through the screen door, "when you managed accounts, could you just take money out if you wanted?" His grandfather looked up from the crossword. "I could have," he said. "That's why they watched me." Owen turned that over. The private field and the watching: two answers to the same problem, one built into the structure and one built into the people. He was not sure which his class needed, or whether a class could need anything at all.

Inside, his grandfather slid a handful of shelled walnuts onto a saucer and carried it out to the porch, setting it between the two laptops without a word. Remi took one and cracked it against the arm of the chair. "So Monday," he said, "when she asks who figured out the failing test, I'm telling her it expected the wrong thing and you're telling them why."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The tour guide led them across the quad with a laminated folder held against her hip, and Sienna counted the bricks of the dormitory they passed because counting was easier than listening. She had been waitlisted at Aldrich, her top choice, eleven days ago. Here at Branford she was admitted, and the deposit of four hundred dollars was due on the first of May.

"Ask your questions now," the guide said, stopping under a copper beech. "This is when I can actually hear you."

A father near the front started to pontificate about his own college days, how he'd chosen a school in three days with nothing but a brochure, and how kids today made everything so complicated. Sienna tuned him out. She was doing arithmetic. Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. She had learned that from a forum at two in the morning, from a user named branfordbound2019 who had lived through it. Which meant that if Aldrich ever wanted her, it would want her after she'd already paid Branford. Four hundred dollars, gone, unless Branford refunded part of it, and the forum said refunds varied.

"Sienna." Flora tugged her sleeve. "You're staring at that tree like it owes you money."

"I'm staring at that tree like it costs four hundred dollars."

Flora laughed, but Rami, standing behind them with his hands in his pockets, didn't. He was waitlisted at his own first choice too, though he'd told almost nobody. He told Sienna because she'd told him first, in the parking lot of their school, the day the decisions came out.

The tour moved into the science building. Glass-walled labs, a poster about summer research, a student asleep at a bench with her cheek on her notebook. The guide said something about the chemistry program being "the hidden gem of the Northeast," and Rami leaned toward Sienna and said, quietly, "That's either true or she's being facetious. I genuinely can't tell anymore. Every sentence on this tour is the best sentence I've ever heard."

"It's her job."

"I know it's her job. That's what makes it worse."

After the tour there was a session in a lecture hall with an admissions officer, a woman introduced as Ms. Ricci, who went over financial aid and housing. During the question period a boy asked whether accepted students could defer a year. Ms. Ricci said yes, with a form. A mother asked about changing majors. Then Sienna raised her hand, and when Ms. Ricci called on her, she heard her own voice ask whether a student who paid the deposit here and then got taken off a waitlist somewhere else in May would get any of the money back.

The room went quiet in the specific way rooms go quiet when a question has cut past the script. Ms. Ricci said that deposits were generally nonrefundable after May 1, that students should only accept a waitlist offer if they were prepared to lose the deposit at the first school, and that families should weigh that carefully. She said it evenly, without softening it, and Sienna wrote down the word nonrefundable in the margin of her folder.

Outside, on the wide stone steps, Flora tried to be helpful. "Four hundred dollars for Aldrich is nothing. That's like, what, textbooks for one semester."

"It's not nothing," Sienna said. "And I might not even get in. I might pay it and lose it and still end up here anyway, four hundred dollars poorer, in the exact same dorm."

"So don't pay it."

"Then I might have nowhere to go."

Rami sat down on the step below them and looked out at the quad, where another tour was forming under the copper beech, another set of parents clutching folders. "It's an honest kind of problem," he said. "Nobody's lying to you. Branford wants you. Aldrich might want you. You just have to decide what four hundred dollars and a maybe are worth against a definite."

"That's the most you've said all day."

"I'm rationing."

Flora elbowed him, and he smiled, and Sienna sat down between them and looked at the folder in her lap, at her own handwriting, nonrefundable, underlined twice. The first of May was nine days away.

"Food before we drive back," Flora said. "There's supposedly a sandwich place two blocks from here that's a hidden gem of the Northeast."

"You're not allowed to use that phrase anymore," Rami said.

"I'm using it facetiously, which is allowed."

Sienna stood, folded the folder, and put it in the side pocket of her backpack where she could feel its corner against her hip through the fabric. "Let's walk," she said. "I want to see the town before I decide anything."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Keeping money as cash has an opportunity cost: the interest or returns it could have earned in a savings account or investment.
story:
The envelope of cash had lived in Autumn's sock drawer for eleven months, two hundred dollars at a time, and today it was going to become a down payment. She counted it once more on the bench outside the phone kiosk: eight hundred and forty dollars, bills soft from handling. Across the atrium, past the food court and the fountain that no one ever threw coins into, there was a small dealer's booth that sold used cars on weekends only, and a gray hatchback with a hand-lettered price she had memorized.

Elise found her there, still in her green kiosk polo, on break with a pretzel. "You actually brought it. The drawer money."

"All of it." Autumn folded the bills back into the envelope. "If I put down cash, the payments are small enough that I can keep the job at the garden center and still save."

Elise broke off a piece of pretzel and didn't eat it. "Mr. Rivera came by yesterday looking for you, by the way. He said something about your mom's account."

Autumn had been avoiding Mr. Rivera for a week, since the evening he'd mentioned, casually, over the fence that his savings earned interest, actual money added to money, just for sitting in the bank. She'd filed it under things adults say to sound wise. But it had followed her to school and to work, a splinter under the skin of every purchase she considered.

They walked toward the booth. Through the glass she could see the hatchback, and a boy from her econ class, Colten, standing beside it with his hands in his pockets, doing the same math she was about to do. Of course he was. He'd been talking about that car since September.

"Go look at something else," Autumn said, only half joking.

"There's a shoe sale," Elise said. "There's always a shoe sale." But she didn't move, and her voice had that careful flatness she used when she knew more than she was saying. "Autumn. What did Rivera say to you, exactly?"

"That cash in a drawer earns nothing. That money in a savings account or an investment earns interest or returns." Autumn recited it the way she recited vocab, then heard herself. "He said it like it was obvious."

"And you're about to hand the drawer money to a man in a mall."

The dealer, when they reached the booth, turned out to be a woman with a clipboard and a lanyard, brisk and cheerful. Colten stepped back to let Autumn go first, which was either courtesy or surrender. The woman quoted the down payment, the monthly figure, the interest rate on the loan, all of it reasonable, all of it in a language Autumn suddenly heard differently. Every number had a shadow behind it, the other number it used to be.

"What's the rate on savings right now?" she asked the woman, feeling foolish.

"At my bank? Doesn't matter to me, but it's something. Better than a drawer." The woman laughed, not unkindly. "You'd be surprised how many kids ask me that this year."

Colten cleared his throat. "That's the thing, though. If she keeps the cash in an account earning interest, and takes the bigger loan, she's paying interest on one side and earning it on the other. If she pays the cash now, she gives up the interest it could have earned. There's a word for that. Mr. Rivera made us learn it." He looked at the ceiling of the mall as if the word were written there. "Opportunity cost."

Autumn turned the phrase over. Every choice had a twin it killed. The boots Elise kept mentioning. The savings account. The car itself, which would carry her to the garden center all winter and to college visits in spring, and which would also, quietly, every month, be the thing her money wasn't.

She walked to the fountain while the dealer helped another customer. Elise followed, chewing slowly, letting the silence do its work. It was their oldest arrangement, an armistice between Elise's directness and Autumn's need to arrive at things herself; Elise would hold the space, and Autumn would fill it.

"Half," Autumn said at last. "I put half down, and half goes into the account. The payments are bigger, but the money that stays keeps earning. And if the car dies, I'm not at zero." She knew the compromise was partly affective, a feeling of safety dressed up as strategy, and she said so. "I can't actually calculate which side wins. I don't know the rates well enough. But I know what I'd regret more."

Colten had drifted over, close enough to hear. "If you're only putting half down, I might still be able to get it first. I have my whole paycheck."

"Then knock yourself out," Autumn said, and was surprised to find she meant it.

At the bank branch by the west entrance, she sat with a new accounts form and a pen that kept skipping. Forty-two dollars a year, the brochure said, on the amount she'd keep, if she left it alone. Not nothing. Not rescue either. She wrote her name, then her sock drawer's whole history of sacrifices, in her head: the concerts skipped, the sales walked past, the envelope thickening in the dark while it earned exactly nothing.

Elise leaned on the counter. "You know Rivera's going to be insufferable about this."

"He already is. That's why I avoided him." Autumn slid the form to the teller. "Tell him the armistice held."

"Tell him yourself. He still wants to talk about your mom's account." Elise's face was careful again, the flatness back, and Autumn understood that this was the subtext under everything: not the car, not the interest, but whatever their neighbor knew that she didn't. She stood, tucked the thinner envelope into her jacket, and turned toward the exit and the street where Mr. Rivera lived.

"I'm going now," she said. "Before I think of a reason not to."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
The shop closed at nine, and it was already twenty past eight, so Mr. Bianchi had begun stacking the chairs on the far side of the room while Laurence and Emerik were still working on their cones. He had said nothing to them directly. He only turned the sign on the register to face the wall and began wiping the counter in long, deliberate strokes, which was his way of imputing a sense of urgency to the evening without having to say a word about it.

They had taken the booth by the window because Emerik liked to watch the cars in the lot, and for most of the last hour he had been narrating them, a gray hatchback that parked crooked, a delivery van that idled for no reason. Laurence had found this easier than talking about herself. Somewhere between the third and fourth car he had reached across the table and put his hand over hers, and she had let it stay, and then she had turned her palm up so that their fingers interlocked, and the small transaction had felt mutual, a little mutualism of gestures, each giving something and getting something back.

"You have foam on your chin," Emerik said.

"I know. I'm keeping it."

"Keeping it."

"It's a look."

Jerry came out from the back with a tub of salty caramel and a scoop, refilling the front bin without looking at them. Jerry was in Laurence's economics class and had watched her fail a quiz on supply curves two days ago, so there was already a version of her in his head that she did not love having at the register tonight. She wiped the foam off her chin with her wrist.

"Ten minutes, kids," Mr. Bianchi said from the counter. He said it to the room.

They finished the cones and Laurence gathered the napkins into a damp ball, and Emerik held the door, and outside the air had gone cool in the way it does after a hot day, all the heat pulled down into the subterranean of the pavement so that you could feel it rising faintly at your ankles. Her mother was picking her up at nine fifteen in the lot behind the bank, which was one block over. Emerik walked with her. At some point he took her hand again, in the open, where anyone could see, and she noticed that she liked it and also that she was performing the liking for him, checking his face to make sure he saw her liking it, and she filed that away as a thing to think about later.

At the corner of the bank lot he stopped.

"I think I'd rather just say goodnight here," he said.

She looked at their hands. He hadn't let go yet, but the sentence had already changed what the hand was, the way a word can change a room before anyone moves the furniture.

"Okay," she said.

"You're not, like, weird about it."

"I'm trying not to be." She was quiet for a second. "We held hands the whole way and that was fine and now it's not, and that's allowed. That's the whole thing. You can withdraw consent at any time, even after you already gave it."

He shrugged, and she could not tell whether the shrug meant yes, obviously, or yes, thank you for saying it out loud, or something in between, a third thing she didn't have a name for. "It was a good date," he said. "I just want to go home, honestly."

"Curfew?"

"Tired. It's not a code."

A car turned into the lot, headlights sweeping across them both, and it was not her mother's car, it was some stranger pulling in to use the ATM. The machine lit up blue and green across the bank's dark windows.

"Can I text you tomorrow?" she asked.

"If you want."

"I'm asking whether you want."

"I don't know yet," Emerik said. "Is that an okay answer?"

She considered it. There was a version of the evening where she decided his answer meant he had never liked her, where she imputed a whole second hidden date to his evening, some other girl, some conversation she wasn't part of, and there was a version where it meant only that he was tired, exactly as he'd said, and the truth was she could not tell which version was real from where she was standing, and maybe no one could, standing at a corner at nine ten at night with ice cream still faint on her tongue. What she did know was smaller and firmer: he had said stop, and stopping had cost her nothing but the walk to the car, and that seemed worth knowing how to do.

"It's an okay answer," she said.

"Goodnight, Laurence."

"Goodnight."

He went one way down the sidewalk and she cut through the lot, and she stood by the bank's side door where her mother would be able to see her under the light. She took out her phone and put it away again without typing anything. The ATM finished with the stranger, who got back in his car, and the machine's screen went dark, and then it lit up again on its own, cycling through some ad for a mortgage rate, bright and then dark and then bright, keeping time with nobody.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
Samuel arrived at the field first, as he always did now, and spread his notebook on the bench beside the goal. The pages were gridded into seven columns, Monday through Sunday, and every box was full. Sprints, sprints, sprints, a game on Saturday, sprints again on Sunday because Sunday had been empty once and the emptiness had looked like failure.

Diana came across the grass with her cleats hanging from one hand. She leaned over his shoulder, read for a moment, and tapped the Sunday column twice. "You've got hard stuff every single day."

"Preseason is in four weeks." He pulled the notebook away an inch, then let it settle back. "I don't have four weeks to waste."

"You have shin splints," she said. "I heard you complaining about them at lunch like an old man."

Skyler jogged up with the ball under one arm, dropped it, and sat on the bench's far end. He was the one who read everything, who printed out articles about professional athletes and quoted them until people walked away. When Samuel slid the notebook toward him without being asked, Skyler frowned at it the way he frowned at badly formatted essays.

"Where's the rest?" Skyler said.

"The rest of what?"

"The rest days. There aren't any." Skyler turned the notebook around so the grid faced Samuel, as though Samuel hadn't drawn it himself. "Look, in periodized training, a season gets divided into cycles. The smallest one, the one you're planning here, is called a microcycle. It usually lasts about one week." He said it flatly, the way he recited everything, then added, "Even the pros don't hammer every day inside one week."

Samuel took the notebook back. He looked at his seven columns and the ink he'd spent on them, and something in him resisted the word rest the way it resisted the substitute teacher's whistle. He had been cut once already, at fourteen, and the coach that year had stood in front of the leftovers and practically eulogized the players who'd been released, praising their attitudes while they carried their bags off the field. He did not intend to be praised like that again.

"That's a lot of theory," he said.

"You're a lot of injured," Diana said.

They made him run it anyway, that afternoon, because practice was practice. Ms. Nolan, who coached the girls' team and sometimes watched the boys' scrimmages from the touchline with her arms crossed, blew her whistle at him when he skipped the warm-up to get extra touches on the ball. He did the warm-up. He resented every second of it, and then, somewhere during the third drill, noticed his shins had gone quiet.

Afterward he sat on the bench with the notebook open and the pen uncapped, and he did not write anything. He thought about the season as Skyler described it, cut into pieces, a week being the smallest piece, and he thought about his own instinct, which was that improvement was a straight line and every empty box a betrayal. Both felt true. He could not make them be the same thing.

He crossed out Sunday entirely. Wrote REST in capitals, then felt the word was too smug, too epicurean for someone with something to prove, and reduced it to lowercase. Then he moved Thursday's sprints to Friday, and put a short warm-up in Thursday's box, and drew a small ugly arrow from Saturday's game back to Monday to remind himself that the week was a wheel, not a staircase. Whether that was right, whether one day of rest was enough or too much, whether Skyler's cycles were science or just another way of being told to slow down, he could not yet say. The proof, if it existed, lived somewhere ahead of him in the season.

Diana and Skyler were walking off the field. Diana turned and cupped her hands around her mouth.

"Samuel. What did you write for Sunday?"

He held up the notebook so the small word showed.

"Rest," she read. Then she laughed, one short note, and pointed at the empty half of the bench beside her. "Well, come on, then. Rest starts with walking home."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller, and shrank further after accounting for family background.
story:
The letter from the honors college had been on the kitchen table for six days, and Audrey had read it four times without opening the reply envelope. The program wanted a two-hundred-dollar deposit by the fifteenth, nonrefundable, and she was still waiting to hear about the scholarship that would decide whether she could afford it at all. Her grandfather, who had moved into the guest room in March after the plant announced his furlough, sat across from her doing the crossword in pencil.

"You know what you ought to do," he said. "Sit on your hands till the money comes through. That's character. They proved it with those kids and the marshmallows. The ones who could wait turned out better later, every time."

"The marshmallow test," Audrey said. It wasn't a question.

"Then you've heard of it."

She had, in Ms. Holloway's class, though not the way he meant it. She pulled her laptop toward her across the table and found the page she'd saved in September, back when she was writing her college essay about self-control and had needed something better than a slogan. "There was a redo of it," she said. "A 2018 replication by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan." She turned the screen so he could see, and he put down the pencil.

"They found the link between waiting and later achievement was much smaller," she read, "and it shrank further after accounting for family background."

Her grandfather put on his reading glasses, which he kept on a cord around his neck, and leaned in. She watched him move his lips slightly over the names. "Much smaller," he repeated.

"Much smaller than the first study made it look."

He sat back. "So you're saying waiting doesn't matter."

"No." She closed the laptop halfway, then thought better of it and opened it again. "I'm saying the kids who ate the marshmallow weren't weak. Some of them had just learned that promises don't always hold. A kid whose mother says there'll be cake Friday and there isn't, that kid eats the marshmallow because waiting is a bad bet where he lives."

Her grandfather was quiet long enough that she could hear the dishwasher in the next room and her mother's radio going upstairs. He picked up the pencil and wrote something in one square, then scratched it out. "When I was laid off the first time, in '82, I ate a lot of marshmallows," he said. "Borrowed against the truck. Your grandmother never let me forget it."

"Was it the wrong thing?"

"It got us through the winter. It cost us the next three years." He folded the crossword over the pencil. "Both of those are true, and I've never sorted out which one matters more."

Audrey thought about the envelope. Waiting was what he was telling her to do, and waiting was also what the kids in the first study supposedly failed at, and the newer study said the whole story was softer than anyone claimed, and none of it told her whether the honors college would still have a seat for her on the sixteenth. She pulled the reply envelope out from under the fruit bowl and looked at the deadline again, as if it might have shifted.

"What's the scholarship worth?" her grandfather asked.

"Full tuition if I get it. Nothing if I don't."

"And when do you hear?"

"They said mid-May. The deposit's due the fifteenth."

He tapped the table twice with the pencil eraser. "So it's not a marshmallow at all. A marshmallow, you eat it or you don't, and either way the story's over. This one, you pay and maybe lose the two hundred, or you wait and maybe lose the seat."

"That's the part I keep going around," she said. "The study doesn't help with the part where the future's actually a gamble. It just says the people who looked patient mostly had better cards to start with." She heard her own voice get sullen on the last word and stopped.

Her mother came down in her robe, looked at the envelope in Audrey's hand, and put water on without asking anyone anything.

"Call them," her grandfather said. "The college. Ask what happens if the deposit's a week late because you're waiting on an outside scholarship. Make them tell you."

Audrey found the number on the letterhead and dialed, and while it rang she slid the two hundred dollars, the birthday money in cash she had been keeping in her desk drawer, out of her pocket and set it on the table between them. Her grandfather looked at it and did not reach for the crossword again.

"Admissions office, this is Alistair," the voice on the phone said.

The community hall smelled of cardamom and burnt wicks before anyone had lit a thing. Mya crouched beside her mother at the long trestle tables, filling brass holders with oil while her cousin handed her cotton wicks one at a time, damp from the jar. Outside, Mika and Braxton waited in Mika's hatchback, engines off, because Mya had said she would come get them when the arrangement was done. That had been forty minutes ago.

"You said friends could come," her mother said, not looking up. She pressed a wick into the oil with one finger, testing its seat.

"I said maybe. I said I'd ask."

"You are asking by texting under the table."

Mya put her phone face down on the tablecloth. Down the hall, the committee women were arguing about whether the stage drapes should be gold or red, and the sound system was giving off that obstreperous hum it made whenever anyone touched the mixer, a groan that filled the room and stopped every conversation until somebody thumped the speaker. Her grandmother sat near the door in her good shawl, saying the rosary of names under her breath, present and elsewhere at once.

The problem was not the friends. The problem was Braxton, specifically, and the thing he had said in the parking lot on Thursday, laughing, not cruelly, which was somehow worse. He'd heard the word Diwali in class and repeated it the way he repeated everything, mangling the vowels, then said it sounded like a diet. Mika had laughed too. Mya had said nothing, and had hated the nothing all weekend, and now she had invited them both because not inviting them felt like agreeing that the whole evening was embarrassing, and inviting them felt like serving it up on a plate.

Ms. De Vries arrived at six with a box of candles for the emergency exit, because fire code required them, and stayed to watch. She was the librarian at the branch near the school and knew Mya from the homework club, knew she wanted to study linguistics, had once spent a whole afternoon explaining phonetics to her with a mirror and the word "light." She stood at the end of the table now with her hands folded behind her back.

"So these are the lamps," she said.

"Diyas," Mya's mother said. "Small oil lamps. For Diwali."

"Is it Hindu?" Ms. De Vries asked, and here Mya answered before her mother could, because this much she knew cold, had known since she was small, that it wasn't only theirs: Hindus, Jains, Sikhs, some Buddhists, all of them lighting the same rows of little flames in homes and temples, light overcoming darkness. She said it plainly, the way you'd say which street you lived on, and her mother nodded once, approving, and Mya felt the strange comfort of facts that do not require you to perform.

"That's the whole point of setting them out in rows," her cousin added, nudging a crooked diya back into line. "One lamp is just a lamp. A hundred is the argument."

Mya looked down the table. The rows ran the length of the hall now, maybe a hundred and twenty small vessels, and she thought about Braxton's mouth shaping the word wrong. She knew exactly how to fix it. She knew the tongue position, the short vowel, the aspirated d. She could coach him in the parking lot in under a minute, the way Ms. De Vries had coached her, and no one would be stigmatized and no one would be corrected in public and everyone would leave feeling fine. And she also knew that she did not want to do it in the parking lot, where the lesson would be a favor done quietly so that nobody had to be seen learning. If he came in, he could stand at the table and ask, and she could answer here, in the open, with her mother's hands right there in the frame.

Whether that was pride or something more useful, she genuinely could not have said. That was the part she kept circling.

She lit the first diya with the long match, cupped the flame against the draft from the door, and walked out to the hatchback. Mika rolled down the window. Braxton was in the back seat with his jacket half on, ready to bolt.

"It's started," Mya said. "Come see the lamps. Or don't. But if you come in, you say the word right, and I'll show you how, in front of everybody."

Braxton looked at her for a long moment, then pulled his sleeve the rest of the way down.

"Say it first," he said. "So I can hear it."

Mya turned toward the lit doorway of the hall, a hundred small flames trembling behind her, and said, "Diwali."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
The waiting room outside the cardiac wing had a vending machine that hummed like a refrigerator left open, and Rose sat beneath a poster of a mountain lake that was meant to be calming. Her grandfather had died at 4:12 in the morning, and by eleven her grandmother had gone home to recuperate, which was the word the nurses used, as though grief were a sprain. Rose had stayed. She wanted, before the room was cleared, to take the tin of peppermints from his bedside table, because he had kept it there for forty years and she could not stand the thought of some orderly's glove closing around it instead of her hand.

Christine arrived first, still in her work polo, smelling of the coffee shop's espresso machine. She had a plan, because Christine always had a plan. "We should go to the viewing together," she said. "And I'll drive, so you don't have to think about it." She unfolded a funeral home brochure she'd already picked up, as if logistics could be assembled in advance like a bookshelf. Rose watched her smooth the glossy page and understood that Christine needed this, needed to be the capable one, and so she said the date out loud even though she didn't know yet if she would be in town.

Carlos came during his free period with two granola bars and his phone already in his hand. In biology he had been the one who printed diagrams, who liked naming things, and he had clearly been reading on the bus. "There's these stages," he said. "Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, 1969, a book called On Death and Dying." He turned the phone toward her. "People always post them after somebody dies. Like a checklist."

Rose read the list twice. Her grandfather had been given three weeks and had taken five days, and during those five days she had not felt denial, had not felt anger, had felt only a flatness like the hallway's fluorescent light. "I don't have any of them," she said. "Is that wrong with me?"

Carlos scrolled, frowning at whatever site he'd found. Then he stopped scrolling. "Huh. It says here she wrote it about the patients. Terminally ill patients facing their own death. Not the families after." He said it slowly, testing it. "So the stages were never about us at all."

They sat with that while the vending machine hummed. Down the corridor a nurse pushed a cart with a squeaking wheel, and somewhere a television murmured game show applause. Rose thought of her grandfather in those five days, how he had refused the pudding and then asked for it, how he had told the night nurse he was tired and meant it in both senses, and she wondered whether he had been moving through those five stages all along, in an order she hadn't recognized. She would never know. That was the part that stayed open, and she let it stay open.

"Ms. Whitehead's here," Christine said suddenly, nodding toward the elevator. Their old English teacher was carrying a casserole dish wrapped in a dish towel, absurd and right at the same time. She had lived next door to the grandparents for a decade; she and Rose's grandfather had argued about property lines with the affection of people who had nothing else to argue about. She didn't say much. She put her hand on Rose's shoulder, mentioned that the iris beds would need splitting this fall whether or not anybody felt like it, and said the casserole was for her grandmother, with instructions to tell her so.

The room was still as they had left it, the bed stripped, the chair at an angle where the chaplain had sat. The tin was there, dented on one corner, warm from the window's afternoon sun as if it had been held. Rose put it in her bag. On the sill, someone long ago had left a paperweight, a thumb of dark igneous glass with a bubble trapped at its center, and she picked that up too, closing her fist around it, the glass holding the heat the same way.

Later, waiting for her mother outside the main doors, Rose tried to explain to Carlos what she had decided, or half decided. "Maybe the stages are real," she said, "just not for the people left behind. Maybe we get something messier. I don't have a word for mine yet." Carlos peeled the wrapper off the second granola bar and handed it to her. "My abuela would say you will," he said. "In like a year. With soup." Rose bit into the bar and, tasting oats and honey, almost laughed.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The United States baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and its bulge on the pyramid has now moved into the retirement ages.
story:
Daniel carried the worksheet folded into his jacket pocket, and every switchback of the trail reminded him it was there, a small square of pressure against his ribs. The assignment was due Monday: analyse the population pyramid of a country of his choosing, and predict, with reasons, whether that country would need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. He had chosen the United States because the data was easy to find, and then found that easy data got him nowhere. He could read the chart. He could not read the future out of it.

"You've gone quiet," Nya said, falling into step beside him. She had the longer stride and had been waiting at each overlook, pretending to study the map. "You do that when something's due."

"It's the pyramid thing," he admitted. "Everyone in class is arguing about whether the answer is schools or nursing homes, like it's a debate you win. Sahar says the whole assignment is rigged, that any pyramid tells you whatever you already decided it tells you. She calls it a revisionist exercise. I think she means you can make the chart say anything."

"She would say that."

Ahead of them, Mr. Do paused where the trail narrowed over a slab of wet rock. He was their neighbour from four doors down, seventy-six years old, and he had invited himself on the hike with a frankness that Daniel's mother had found funny and Daniel had found, initially, gratuitous. Now he stood with his hand out, not for help exactly, but near enough to the offer of it that Daniel took his arm without either of them naming what had happened.

"Steady," Mr. Do said. "The rock doesn't care how confident you are." He crossed, then turned to watch Nya cross, and then Daniel, as though the order of their safety were a matter he had scheduled.

At the overlook they stopped, as hikers do, and Mr. Do unwrapped a sandwich and offered halves before taking his own. Daniel took his worksheet out, more for something to do with his hands than anything, and smoothed it against his knee. The pyramid was printed small, bars narrowing and widening up the page, and beside it his notes had stalled at a question mark.

"Population pyramid," Mr. Do said, reading upside down with the ease of a man who had spent thirty years reading upside down. "Those things used to be actual pyramids. Wide at the bottom, all those children. Now they look more like a chimney with a bulge in it."

"Which part is the bulge?" Nya asked, leaning over. She was the one in their group who asked questions other people were embarrassed to ask, and Daniel had watched, over four years of shared classes, how the questions she asked aloud sutures a conversation together that would otherwise have fallen apart into separate silences.

Mr. Do pointed without touching the page, at the middle and upper bars. "That's me," he said. "Right there. The baby boom generation was born between 1946 and 1964, and that whole bulge has moved up into the retirement ages now. We're the fat part near the top of the chimney."
