Daniel looked at the bars Mr. Do had indicated, and then at Mr. Do, who was chewing his sandwich half and looking out at the valley, where the haze sat in layers like something poured. In his notes the bulge had been a shape. It had not once, in three days of staring, occurred to him that it was the man beside him, who had asked for the hike, who had crossed the wet rock with an arm held out.

"So in thirty years," Daniel said slowly, "that whole band is at the very top. Narrow bars below it, my parents, then me, then whoever's after me." He turned the pencil in his fingers. "The top of the pyramid gets heavy and the bottom doesn't refill itself unless something changes. That's nursing homes. That's the obvious answer. The bars say so."

"But?" Nya said.

"But Sahar's not wrong that a chart is an argument somebody drew. The bars are averages, and the bars don't say who any of them are. If I write only nursing homes, I'm deciding the whole bulge is a burden. If I write only schools, I'm pretending the top of the page isn't there." He wrote something in the margin, crossed it out, wrote again. "Maybe the honest answer is that it's both, in different places, and the pyramid can't tell you which place."

"Then say that," Mr. Do said. He folded the wax paper from his sandwich into a neat square and put it in his pocket rather than leaving it. "You'll get marked down, probably. Teachers want an answer. But you'll have told the truth, and the truth has a way of being useful later." He stood, brushed crumbs from his knees, and held out his hand to help Nya up. "Come on. Three more switchbacks and we can see the lake."

Daniel folded the worksheet along its old creases and put it back in his pocket, the question mark still there but smaller now, crowded out by a sentence he had actually written. He shouldered his pack and took Mr. Do's other arm at the lip of the rock, and the three of them went up into the pines, the old man setting the pace.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The gown arrived in a plastic envelope that smelled faintly of the warehouse, and Charlotte's mother ironed it on the kitchen table with a towel laid over the satin so it wouldn't scorch. Charlotte sat across from her with a pen, transcribing names onto place cards for the party afterward, because her handwriting was the only one in the house anybody trusted. Aunt this, cousin that, Jessy and Lyvia with little laurels drawn beside their names because they'd earned something ridiculous. She wrote her own name last, on the card for the seat at the head of the table, and then set the pen down and looked at it for a while.

"You're allowed to be sad about it," her mother said, not looking up from the iron. "But you're not allowed to be rude to your grandmother tomorrow."

"I wasn't going to be rude to Grandma."

"You were going to be quiet in a way that reads as rude."

Charlotte laughed despite herself, which she suspected had been the point. The truth was she had been dreading tomorrow for a week, and the dread had a specific shape. It wasn't the speeches or the heat of the auditorium or the fact that her cousin had already texted three times about parking. It was that at eleven forty in the morning, when the principal called her name and she walked across the stage, everything she could see from that stage would already be over. Four years compressed into a handshake and a photographer. She hadn't said this out loud because it sounded self-pitying, and because her mother had paid for the cake.

Jessy came over that evening with Lyvia, who had been on again with her boyfriend and then off again within the same afternoon and wanted to tell the whole saga. They sat on the garage steps while Charlotte's mother brought out lemonade without being asked, which Lyvia accepted like medicine. Lyvia's account of the breakup involved layered machinations on the part of the boy's former girlfriend, a campaign of screenshots and strategic silences, and though Charlotte privately thought the ex-girlfriend was probably just as confused as anyone, she let Lyvia have the drama. It was the night before graduation; everyone deserved their own version of the story.

"You're doing the face," Jessy said when Lyvia had gone inside to fix her eyeliner.

"What face."

"The face you did when we closed the yearbook. The saturnine one, like you're in a play about a doomed queen." Jessy nudged her with a shoulder. "It's tomorrow and you look like you're going to a funeral."

"It's not a funeral." Charlotte turned the lemonade glass in her hands. "It's just, I keep thinking that thing ends and nothing starts. Everyone keeps saying congratulations like something happened to me. Nothing happened. I just... finished showing up."

Lyvia came back out, wiping under one eye with her finger, and both of them looked at her because she had gone very still, the way she did when she'd remembered a homework assignment due in an hour. "Wait," Lyvia said. "What did Ms. Kaya call it? In assembly, in the fall. Commencement. It means beginning."

"Okay," Charlotte said.

"No, that's the whole thing. That's why they call the ceremony that. Because you're beginning a new status. Like being a bachelor or a master. That's why the word got used for graduations." Lyvia sat back down between them, pleased with herself. "I only remember because I thought it was a typo on the program."

Charlotte said nothing for a minute. Across the yard Ms. Kaya's kitchen light was on, and through the window she could see the older woman moving slowly between counter and stove, and it occurred to her that Ms. Kaya had watched her carry the trash out every Tuesday since she was nine, and that Ms. Kaya would probably still be doing that after tomorrow, and that Charlotte would not be there to wave at, and that this was somehow the thing that made her throat hurt. But the word turned over in her head anyway. Beginning. Not an ending with a party attached.

"It's still the last time we all sit in one room," she said finally. "That part's true no matter what the word means."

"Obviously that part's true," Jessy said. "You can hold two things. You're allowed." She drained her glass and stood. "Come on. Tassel practice."

They practiced in the driveway under the porch light, Lyvia counting them across an imaginary stage, Jessy walking with exaggerated gravity until Lyvia cracked up, until Charlotte's mother came out to ask what was so funny and got drafted as principal, calling their names with mock solemnity while the moths circled the light above the door. When it was Charlotte's turn she moved the tassel from right to left the way they'd been told, and then stood there a second longer than she needed to, in the dark, in her jeans, holding nothing.

Inside, the place cards were still fanned across the table. She found hers and turned it face down, then turned it back over, and left it where it was. In the morning she would pin her hair the way her mother liked and she would not be rude to her grandmother, and at eleven forty her name would be called, and whether it felt like a door closing or a door opening she could not yet say. From the kitchen her mother called, "Charlotte, the iron's still warm if you want your other dress done."

"Coming," she said, and went in.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
story:
Sophie had promised herself she would not be nervous, which was the first sign that she was. She spread the laminated current map on the flat top of her cooler, weighted the corners with shells, and looked out over the water where the assignment was supposed to be happening. Ms. Lombardi had said the beach was the right place to study the ocean, and had said nothing else, which Sophie chose to believe was confidence in her and not indifference.

She had sprained her ankle three weeks ago at track, and it had recuperated just enough that walking on sand felt like a negotiation. That was her excuse, if anyone asked, for sitting still while Derick and Jagger were down at the waterline throwing a flat stone back and forth like a Frisbee. Nobody asked. The stone kept dropping into the foam, and Jagger kept retrieving it, and their argument about whether the game counted if the stone kept getting wet carried up the beach on the wind.

The map showed arrows, red and blue, threaded across the Atlantic. Sophie traced the American coast with her finger: Florida, then Georgia, then the Carolinas. The warm red arrow ran close along the shore the whole way, and then, off Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, it left the coast entirely and bent northeast across the open ocean. She had drawn her own version of this last night from memory, and she had put the turn at Florida. She remembered now, clearly, that she had put it at Florida. Her notebook was in the car as proof, or would have been, if she went to get it.

Derick jogged up the beach and dropped onto the sand beside the cooler, breathing hard. "You're studying on a Saturday," he said. "That's a choice."

"It's due Monday." She tapped the place where the arrow left the coast. "Why here? Why not somewhere south, where the water's warmer?"

"Maybe the ocean just does what it wants." He picked up one of her weighting shells and turned it over. "Like in ethics. Jagger keeps going on about utilitarianism in debate, greatest good for the greatest number, but the ocean doesn't care about the greatest number. It doesn't care about anything."

Sophie said that was exactly the kind of answer that got a C, and Derick said a C was fine with him, and they were both quiet for a moment. The water near the shore was turbid, brown-green where the waves had churned up the sand, and beyond the sandbar it went dark and clean, and Sophie looked at the dark part and tried to make the arrow in her mind leave a coast she could not see.

Ms. Lombardi had driven her own car and was walking the tideline with her shoes in her hand. Sophie watched her approach and rehearsed a question, and when Ms. Lombardi stopped at the edge of the towel, Sophie asked whether the warm current turned at Cape Hatteras because the coast turned away from it, or whether the coast had nothing to do with it. She had decided in the last hour that she preferred her own question to any answer, and she almost hoped Ms. Lombardi wouldn't take it from her.

"That's a Monday question," Ms. Lombardi said, which was the kind of thing that sounded like a compliment and might not be. "Tell me what you'd say to someone who thinks Britain is warm because it's an island."

Sophie said she would point at the arrow crossing the whole Atlantic, carrying warm water northeast, and say that the warmth had to come from somewhere, and that somewhere was the Gulf Stream, and that the Gulf Stream left the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. She heard the sentence come out of her and thought it sounded less like her own idea than like the map speaking through her, which was either a failure or the whole point of studying.

"So it warms the north of Europe," Jagger said, arriving with the wet stone in his hand, having apparently listened from ten feet away. "So England's not my problem in December. Good to know."

"The map says northeast across the Atlantic," Sophie said. "Past us, toward them." She put her finger on the far edge of the map, where the red arrow faded into the latitude of northern Europe, and Derick took the wet stone from Jagger and threw it, flat and low, out over the turbid water, and the three of them watched to see how far it would go.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The U-Haul's ramp made a sound like a dying accordion when her father kicked it flat, and Noemie counted the boxes again, as if counting could destabilize the fact that they were really here, in a town where the water tower had a smiley face painted on it and she knew nobody. Eleven days before school started, she had learned the names of three streets, one cashier, and a dog that barked at her sneakers. That was the entire census of her new life.

Back home, in the apartment they'd left, there had been a rotation of voices through her door most evenings. Priya arguing about films. Rosa and her drumming on the radiator. She had assumed, in the careless way you assume gravity, that the noise would follow her. It had not. Her phone sat on the windowsill showing a thread that had gone quiet for six days, then nine, then twelve, the messages from her old friends thinning the way rain thins before it stops.

On the Thursday before school, she sat in the empty kitchen eating cereal from a mug and listening to her mother's radio, which was tuned to the news out of habit rather than conviction. A report mentioned the Surgeon General. Noemie looked up at the word, because Vivek Murthy's name had shown up in her civics class once, on a slide about public health. In May 2023, the anchor said, Murthy had issued an advisory, and Noemie turned the word over, advisory, liking how official it sounded for something that couldn't be enforced, and then the anchor said the rest of it: the advisory described loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. Noemie set down the mug. An epidemic. Like something you could catch, or already had.

She walked to the dollar store to buy a notebook, mostly so she'd have somewhere to walk. The cashier was the one whose name she knew, Tasha on the badge, and Tasha said the humidity was criminal, and Noemie said it really was, and that small exchange carried her half a block before it ran out. She wondered whether other people were walking around holding the same silence, whether the epidemic had a shape you could see if you stood far enough back. She wondered, with a mild scientific curiosity she didn't entirely trust, whether she was a data point.

School opened on a Tuesday. Her homeroom teacher, Ms. Cruz, had them introduce themselves with one true fact and one false one, a game Noemie found unexpectedly good, since it assumed everyone was interesting and everyone was lying. A boy named Santiago said he'd been stung by a jellyfish, and later, when the teacher asked them to write about a current event, he leaned over Noemie's desk and said, "I did the Surgeon General thing. Loneliness. Weird assignment for a math teacher, right?"

"You did that one too?" Noemie said.

"Everyone did that one. It was everywhere. My abuela clipped it out of the newspaper." He tapped her notebook. "What'd you write?"

She hadn't written anything yet. She had the radio version in her head, the advisory, the epidemic, the whole sentence intact because it had nowhere else to go. "I don't know," she said. "I heard it on the news and it kind of stuck."

At lunch she found herself at a table with Santiago and a girl named Yara and a quiet boy called Hashim, who was reading a paperback with a broken spine and answered questions in full paragraphs when he answered at all. Santiago recounted the jellyfish story, which turned out to be true, and then a debate started about whether true facts were more interesting than false ones, and Hashim said the whole game was pedantry, which Santiago took as a compliment, and the argument ate the whole lunch period. Noemie contributed two sentences and one laugh that surprised her with its loudness.

That evening she sat on her bed with the phone in her hand for a long time. The advisory had given the silence a name, and the name made it both smaller and larger, the way a diagnosis does. She thought about her mother's affective way of answering "how was your day" with her whole face, and about Hashim who spoke in paragraphs, and about the difference between being alone and being lonely, which weren't the same thing even though the report had mentioned both. She didn't have that worked out. She noted it as an open question, the way Ms. Cruz had taught them in one class and Santiago had mocked in another.

She called Rosa. Not texted, called, which she hadn't done since eighth grade, and Rosa picked up on the fourth ring and said, "Who died?" in the joking voice that meant nothing had died, and then, "Wait, are you okay?"

"I heard this thing on the news," Noemie said. "In May 2023 the Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, put out an advisory. He called loneliness and isolation an epidemic in the United States."

"An epidemic," Rosa repeated. "Like the flu."

"Like the flu," Noemie said, "except you fix it by calling people, apparently, which is what I'm doing, so you're welcome, you're my public health intervention."

There was the sound of Rosa's laugh and then the sound of Rosa's house, a door, a sibling, the radiator that Noemie could picture exactly. They talked for forty minutes about nothing important, and it didn't fix anything, exactly, because the new town was still the new town and tomorrow she would still be the new girl, but the epidemic, if that's what it was, had one fewer active case for the evening, or at least a milder one.

At school the next morning, Santiago was explaining to Hashim, at unnecessary length, why the jellyfish had technically won the encounter. Noemie slid into the seat across from them and unpacked her lunch, and when she looked up, Hashim had pushed his paperback aside and was watching her with the mild, waiting expression of someone about to ask how her day was, and she said, "Ask me the true-fact question. I've been practicing one."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
Peyton had promised her mother she would pass the calculus quiz on Friday, and by Wednesday afternoon the promise felt like a stone in her shoe. The problem on the board involved a polynomial, some long animal of an equation with an x cubed in it, and the question underneath it: find the maximum. Ms. Ong had said the words once, quickly, near the end of class, and then the bell had swallowed them. Now Peyton sat in the cafeteria with Patricia and Karlee, staring at the same problem photocopied onto a worksheet that had already gone soft at the edges from being folded and unfolded.

"I think the maximum is at x equals five," Patricia said, tapping the page. "That's where the graph is highest on my calculator."

"You're guessing," Peyton said. "You're scrolling through and eyeballing the top."

"Estimating," Patricia said, with dignity.

Karlee, who had finished her own worksheet during lunch and was now drawing a border of tiny stars around it, leaned over. "Ms. Ong said something about the derivative changing signs. I wrote it down. I wrote down, where the derivative changes, that's the answer." She turned her notebook around so they could see the sentence, underlined twice, slightly smeared.

That was not enough, and Peyton knew it. A derivative could change from negative to positive just as easily as the other way, and one of those had to be a maximum and one had to be something else, and if she picked the wrong one on Friday she would lose the points she needed. She took a napkin from the dispenser, smoothed it against the table, and borrowed Karlee's pen.

She had already differentiated the polynomial for homework, so she copied the derivative onto the napkin and set it equal to zero. Two roots came out: x equals two and x equals five. "So there are two candidates," she said. Patricia made a skeptical noise and went to buy more fries, and Karlee went with her, which left Peyton alone with the napkin, the hum of the cafeteria undulating around her in waves of noise that rose and fell without ever quite breaking.

She drew a number line across the napkin and marked two and five on it. Then she tested a value to the left of two, plugging it into the derivative, and got a negative number. She tested a value between two and five and got a positive number. So between the two candidates, the derivative changed from negative to positive, and if she thought about what that meant for the original function, it had to be falling and then rising, which made a valley, a low point, not what she wanted. She tested a value to the right of five. Positive. And to the left of five, the value she had already found: positive there too, all the way through the middle stretch.

She sat back. On the left side of five the derivative was positive; on the right side of five it was negative. Positive to negative. She pictured the original function climbing up to that point and then descending after it, rising and then falling, and something in her chest loosened. That had to be the top. That was the maximum, at x equals five, and it was not a guess anymore, it was a sign chart on a napkin with arrows drawn on it, up into the point and down out of it.

When Patricia and Karlee came back with fries, Peyton turned the napkin around. "Look. On this side the derivative is positive and on that side it's negative. The function rises and then falls, so five is a local maximum." She paused, because she wanted to say it right. "That's the first derivative test."

"Which is what I said," Patricia said. "Five."

"You said five because you scrolled with your thumb," Peyton said. "I'm saying five because of this." She held up the napkin, which had a grease shadow forming at one corner. She was honest enough, inside herself, to admit what stayed uncertain: she had not checked whether five was the highest point everywhere or only nearby, and Ms. Ong had used the word "local" twice in class for reasons Peyton did not yet fully understand, and Friday's quiz might ask about a minimum too, where the signs would have to run the other way, negative to positive, and she would have to think it through again from the start rather than trust a memorized picture. But she had the picture. That was more than she had had at lunch.

On Friday she sat two rows from the window with the quiz face down in front of her, and when Ms. Ong, choleric that morning over a broken projector and a boy who had forgotten his textbook twice in one week, finally said "begin," Peyton turned the paper over. The polynomial on the second question was different from the practice one, longer, with a coefficient she had not seen before. She differentiated it anyway, set it equal to zero, and then, before touching her calculator, drew a quick number line in the margin. She wrote the signs at each interval, positive, then positive again, then negative, and drew a small arrow rising into the middle point and a small arrow falling away from it. Outside the window, someone was raking leaves across the track in long dark lines. Peyton circled her answer and moved on.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
The canoe dock at Camp Wenatchee smelled of cedar and sunscreen, but Ashley had claimed a corner of the craft shed instead, her laptop balanced on a folding table between the paddles and the coil of rope. Mr. Bighorn, who ran the camp's small programming elective and spoke perhaps forty words a day, had handed her a slip of paper on Monday morning with three lines on it. Build a class, he had written. Private fields. Getters. Then test it. That was all. Ashley had stared at the paper through the whole swim period, less annoyed than curious, the way she got when a puzzle refused to tell her whether it was easy or hard.

She had not written a class before. At school she had copied code off the board, changed numbers, watched things print. Here there was nothing to copy. She typed a class called Camper, gave it a field for a name, and then hesitated, because the slip said private, and she wasn't sure what privacy meant to a machine. She made the field private anyway, the way you follow a rule before you understand it, and when she tried to set the name from another file, the compiler underlined her line in red like a teacher catching her cheating.

"You look like someone stole your lunch," Tucker said from the doorway, dripping lake water onto the gravel floor. He was in her elective, a connoisseur of other people's errors, the kind of person who collected screenshots of other campers' broken programs the way some kids collected baseball cards. He leaned over her screen, and when he saw the red underline, his whole face brightened. "You're trying to touch it from outside."

"Touch what?"

"The field. The name thing. You made it private, so it's locked." He pulled a crate over and sat. "You have to ask politely. Write a getter."

She had inured herself to being corrected by Tucker over three weeks of camp, and the sting had worn down to something almost useful. She wrote a method called getName that returned the field, made it public, and ran the test file again. This time the name printed, clean and ordinary, and Ashley sat back and looked at it, because it had worked and she still didn't know why the trouble had been necessary. Why not just leave the field open? Why lock a door and then hand everyone a key?

Mr. Bighorn came through the shed looking for a wrench, saw her screen, and stopped for exactly four seconds. "Good," he said. Then, at the door, without turning around: "Encapsulation." He left before she could ask him anything, which was how he ran the elective, a taciturn man who treated explanation as something you earned.

"Encapsulation," Sullivan repeated that evening, sprawled on the picnic table outside the mess hall. Sullivan had been at the camp two summers and claimed to know everything, though mostly what Sullivan knew was which counselor left the canteen unlocked. "Means you hide stuff. Like a wrapped present."

"A present you can open," Ashley said. "The getter opens it."

"Then what's the point of the wrapping?"

The question followed her to breakfast the next morning. She carried it to the craft shed, and there she did something that Mr. Bighorn had not asked for and that she could not entirely explain afterward, not even to herself. Her Camper class stored the name as a single String, one field, one getter. She selected the field, changed its type to an ArrayList of String, so that a camper could hold a first name and a nickname and a preferred name all at once, and then she waited for everything to break. The whole point of changing things, in her experience, was that changing them broke other code. She held her breath and ran the test file.

The name printed. First name, nickname, all of it, exactly as before.

Tucker was the one who understood first, or at least who understood it in a way he could hold onto. He had wandered into the shed looking for the duct tape and found Ashley staring at her screen with her hands flat on the table, as if the laptop might bolt. When she told him what she had done, that she had changed how the class kept its data and nothing outside it had so much as flinched, he went quiet in a manner entirely unlike him. He read her test file. He read her getter. He read the field declaration twice. Somewhere in that second reading, the shape of the thing assembled itself in his mind, and he thought: all the code outside never touched the field, ever, not once, only the getter, only the asking politely. That was why it hadn't broken. You could gut the inside of the thing, rearrange it completely, and as long as the getter still handed back a name, nobody outside would even know anything had changed. He thought of the paddles racked in the shed, each one identical from the handle end, whatever wood and glue held inside.

"Nobody depends on how it stores it," he said out loud, slowly, testing each word. "They just use it."

"That's what the hiding is for," Ashley said. "It's not wrapping paper. It's a wall. The other code doesn't get to care what's behind it." She was already typing, and he watched her add a third field, an age stored one way, tested and returned another, and watched the outside world go on asking its simple questions and getting its simple answers, blind and undamaged. It occurred to him that this was the opposite of fragile. He had spent the summer believing that everything in programming snapped when you looked at it sideways.

She did not feel finished, though. There was a question she could not close, sitting somewhere behind her ribs: whether the wall was honest. The class told the outside world a small, tidy story about itself, and the tidiness was a kind of lie, because behind the getter there was mess and change and her own frantic rearranging. Maybe all good things worked like that. Maybe people did too, though she wasn't ready to say so out loud, and Mr. Bighorn, who might have known, had already gone down to the water.

At the final showcase on Friday, parents drifting between tables of pinecone art and canoe diagrams, Ashley's laptop displayed a plain line of text: a camper's three names, printed as if they had always been one. Mr. Bighorn stood at her table for nearly a full minute, the longest he had stood anywhere all summer. He looked at her test file, then at the changed field, then at her.

"Run it again," he said.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
story:
The county library smelled like carpet cleaner and old paper, and Laura had claimed the table by the window because its afternoon light kept her honest. She spread the photocopies flat: the mock court assignment, the case packet, two legal pads, one labeled FOR and one labeled AGAINST. Ms. Nakamura had insisted everyone argue both sides. "If you can't make the other side's best case," she had said on Monday, "you don't understand your own." It had sounded like wisdom then. Now it felt like being asked to stand in two rooms at once.

Colton dropped into the chair across from her and slid a granola bar across the table like a bribe. "You're doing the free speech one," he said. It wasn't a question. "I got search and seizure. Lucky you. Free speech means you can basically say whatever happens to be in your head."

"That's not the rule," Laura said, and heard her mother's teacher-voice come out of her, the one she'd sworn off last year after the incident at the dinner table. She swallowed it. "There's an old line about it. Falsely shouting fire in a theatre, causing a panic. That speech, the Court said, isn't protected."

Colton peeled the wrapper down. "So there's a line somewhere and nobody knows where."

"Everybody thinks they know where," Laura said. "That's the problem."

He left for the stacks eventually, and she worked the FOR side first, because it came easily, the way things come when you already believe them. She wrote three pages before Addyson arrived with her own packet and an iced coffee she wasn't supposed to have in the library, condensation pooling on the tabletop like evidence.

Addyson read over Laura's shoulder, which Laura normally hated but permitted in Addyson's case. "You quoted the fire thing," Addyson said. "In your free speech brief. Like it's the Constitution."

"It's a Supreme Court case. Schenck, 1919. Justice Holmes wrote it."

Addyson turned Laura's legal pad toward herself and tapped the citation. "And you read what the case was actually about?"

Laura had read the packet's excerpt, the famous sentence, the part everyone quoted. She had not, she realized, gone past it. She felt the specific heat of being caught in a shortcut. Addyson was already typing on her phone, then turned the screen around: a scanned page, the case name at the top, the opinion written by Holmes in 1919. The man had been convicted under it. He had printed leaflets urging resistance to the draft, and the Court upheld the conviction. The theatre line, the one Laura had built a paragraph on, came from an opinion that put a man in prison for pamphlets.

"That's the other side's whole argument, isn't it," Laura said slowly. "Who said it and when."

"Colton's side," Addyson confirmed, if Colton drew the same pairing in the bracket. "Whoever he is. You just handed him a knife."

Laura sat back. The light through the window had gone long and orange, the way it did before the librarians started their closing circuit. She thought about how quickly an idea could calcify, how a sentence repeated often enough stops being an argument and becomes furniture, something you lean on without checking whether it holds. She had done that. She started a new page in the AGAINST pad.

The trouble was that both pages were now true to her. The fire line was a real limit, stated by a real justice in a real case, and it had also been the reasoning of a court that jailed a pamphleteer, which was exactly what the free speech side was supposed to be afraid of. She tried to hold both at once and felt something like the homeostasis Ms. Nakamura was always describing in biology club, a body keeping two opposing forces in balance, not by resolving them but by continuously adjusting. Except Laura wasn't sure a mind was supposed to work like a body. She wrote: The rule survives. Its first use does not. Then she crossed it out and wrote: The rule's first use is part of the rule. Then she crossed that out too, and left the question sitting on the page, unanswered, honest.

Colton came back with a book on constitutional history and found her surrounded by paper. "You look like you lost a fight," he said.

"I found out who wrote the fire line. For Schenck, 1919, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes. Falsely shouting fire in a theatre, causing a panic. Not protected." She said it flat, all of it, and watched his face arrive at the same place hers had.

"Wait," Colton said. "That's from the case where the guy went to prison for leaflets?" He laughed, one short note. "I was going to argue free speech is unlimited. That's dead."

"That's not what I'm saying."

"Then what are you saying?"

Laura looked at her two legal pads, the FOR and the AGAINST, each of them now stronger than the version she'd started with, neither of them complete. "I'm saying the most parsimonious argument isn't always the true one. A simple line feels like an answer. It might just be a shortcut." She closed the AGAINST pad and squared it on top of the other. "I don't know where the line is. I know who drew the first one, and why, and it's complicated."

The overhead lights clicked off in the far section, Ms. Nakamura's signal that the library was closing in fifteen minutes. Addyson drained her coffee. Colton flipped open his book to the index and ran a finger down the column.

"Schenck," he read. "Page two sixty-one." He looked up. "Tomorrow, you take the free speech side and I'll take the government. Best argument wins."

"Both my arguments are good," Laura said, stacking the pages.

"Then argue both," Colton said, and held out his hand for the photocopied excerpt, and she gave it to him.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
Nevaeh had been avoiding the fast section of the scales sheet for three days, which was its own kind of skill, the kind her mother would have pathologized if she'd known about it, calling it avoidance instead of what it actually was: a private negotiation with embarrassment. The band room was empty except for her and the wall of mirrors along the back, where forty versions of herself sat with forty rented trumpets, all of them slightly out of tune.

"You're still here," Alina said from the doorway, her flute case balanced on one hip. "Ms. Marino said practice rooms were open till five."

"I'm practicing," Nevaeh said, which was technically true if you counted playing the first two lines of the exercise forty times and stopping every time the third line approached.

Alina dropped onto the riser beside her and opened her case without ceremony. "Mind if I warm up? You're going to hear some very bad sounds."

"Yours are always good sounds."

"That's because you've never heard me learn anything new." Alina blew a thin, wobbling note and winced at it comfortably, the way you'd wince at a stubbed toe, already knowing it would fade.

Nevaeh watched her and felt something shift, small and specific. She set the metronome on the music stand, the old kind with the dial, and turned it down past 120, past 100, all the way to 60. The pendulum swung wide and slow, like something breathing in its sleep.

"Sixty," Alina said, glancing over. "That's one beat per second. Sixty beats per minute."

At that speed the passage stopped being a passage and became a set of separate decisions. Nevaeh placed each note inside its own second, and for the first time she could hear which fingers were lying to her, the third valve combination arriving late every single time, a small traitor in an otherwise loyal hand. She had thought the problem was speed. The problem was that she'd never actually known the notes; she'd only known them at a gallop, where mistakes could hide inside momentum.

When she pushed the dial back up to 92, the passage came apart again, though differently now, coming apart at the seams instead of in the middle. Ms. Marino appeared in the doorway with a stack of folders and watched for a moment without coming in. "That's the right kind of ugly," she said. "Keep it." Then she was gone down the hallway, and Nevaeh understood she'd been listened to without being rescued, which was somehow both worse and better.

Brayden stuck his head in twenty minutes later, looking for his forgotten backpack, and found it under the percussion cabinet. He lingered by the door, thumbing the strap. "I thought you sounded better last week," he said, meaning it kindly.

"Last week I was faking the fast part."

He looked at the metronome, its pendulum still swinging at its slowest, most patient setting, and something crossed his face like weather. "Huh," he said. "I always just play it fast until it works." He picked up the backpack, put it down again, and took his clarinet out instead, sitting on the far riser without asking. For a while the two of them worked in opposite corners of the room, both of them slow, both of them deliberate, and the afternoon light through the high windows turned the dust into something diaphanous and drifting, unbothered by any of them.

Nevaeh knew a saying her grandfather used, some aphorism about slow being smooth and smooth being fast, and she had always filed it under things old people say that sound wise but mean nothing. She was no longer sure it meant nothing. She was also not sure that sixty beats a minute would get her to the audition in three weeks, or whether patience was a virtue or just a slower route to the same failure. Both of those things could be true at once, and she sat with that for the length of one full swing of the pendulum, then another, then set her embouchure and began again, watching in the mirror as forty versions of herself lifted their horns together.

"Count us in," Alina said.

"One," said Nevaeh, "and."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search works only on sorted data: it compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half of the list that cannot contain it.
story:
The dictionary at her grandmother's house was the size of a breadbox, and Jade had spent every summer of her childhood failing to look things up in it. She would start at A and page forward, and by the time she reached the middle of the C's her grandmother would have found the word already, opening the book near the back with a practiced thumb. "You're fighting the book," her grandmother said once, tapping the spine. "Let the book fight itself." Jade was seventeen now, back for the last week before college, and she had a laptop open on the kitchen table and a problem she couldn't solve.

The coding club's membership list was the problem, four hundred and eleven names in a file, and every term Henry ran his search on it and every term it missed people. He had written it himself, proudly, and he'd shown it to her on the bus: check the middle name, he'd said, and if what you want comes after it, throw away the first half, check the middle of what's left, throw away half again. It sounded like magic to Jade at the time. It also, apparently, didn't work, because Jazmin had texted her a screenshot that morning: SEARCHING FOR VARGAS. NOT FOUND. MEMBER VARGAS DENIED ENTRY TO POTLUCK. Jazmin was disaffected about the potluck, and Jade didn't blame her.

She started by retyping Henry's code from memory, then stopped, because retyping wasn't the same as understanding. Instead she pulled the dictionary across the table and looked up a word she already knew, just to watch her grandmother's method work. She opened near the middle. The page said L. L came after the word she wanted, so the word had to be in the first half, and she lifted the whole back half of the book away in one motion, a thousand pages discarded without regret. Then the middle of what was left, then again, then her finger landed on the entry, seven openings of the book instead of four hundred.

"That's the thing," she said out loud, to the kitchen. The dictionary, she realized, was sorted; that was what made the discarding legal. You could only throw away a half if you knew, for certain, that the half couldn't hold what you wanted, and you only knew that because the words ran in order. Henry's file, she was nearly sure, did not. She'd seen it once, names marching down the screen in the order people had signed up, Abiodun beside Zimmer, Chen wedged between Okafor and Brennan like a guest at the wrong wedding.

Mr. He, the neighbor, came by at five for the tomatoes he'd been promised, and found her sorting names into two piles with her grandmother's card table as a workspace. "Registry for something?" he asked. "Binary search," she said. "It only works on sorted data. Henry's list isn't sorted, that's all." Mr. He nodded slowly, as if this confirmed something he'd long suspected about Henry, and stole a tomato while offering, in exchange, an opinion about how young people kept their information in what he called "a state of ontological chaos," meaning, as far as Jade could tell, that nobody alphabetized anything anymore. Her grandmother said his ontology was fine but his tomato-taking was criminal, and Mr. He laughed so hard he had to sit down.

Jade wrote the sorted function that evening, a merge sort from a library tutorial she only half understood, and felt the honest unease of using a tool she couldn't yet build. She liked understanding things from the ground up; her grandmother, who could find any word in seven moves, had never once explained the principle aloud. Maybe some knowledge worked that way, resident in the hands before the head. But she couldn't just externalize the whole fix onto a library either, not without being able to say why the old version failed. She ran the search on the sorted list herself. VARGAS, FOUND. FOUR COMPARISONS. She ran it for Abiodun, for Chen, for herself. Found, found, found.

The club met on Thursdays in Mr. He's garage, which he lent them for reasons involving his grandson's abandoned robotics kit and a soft spot for teenagers with laptops. Jade brought the sorted file on a flash drive and let Henry run his own search, unchanged, on it. He typed VARGAS, hit enter, and stared at the screen when the name appeared. "It works," he said, injured. "It works now. What did you change?"

"Nothing in your code," Jade said. "Your code was always fine. The list was the problem. It wasn't sorted." Henry scrolled up through the old file, and she watched him see it, the Abiodun next to the Zimmer, the Chen in the wrong country entirely, his face moving from betrayal toward something more like wonder. Jazmin raised her hand from the back, where she was guarding the leftover potluck hummus. "Motion to formally readmit Vargas," she said. "Seconded by everyone who got hummus."

Jade seconded it, then pulled her laptop over to show Henry the dictionary trick, opening the breadbox-sized book at random. "Look," she said, and split the world in half.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
Samuel spread his notes across the kitchen table and pushed the fruit bowl aside to make room, which his mother would notice later and say nothing about, the way she said nothing about most things lately. The session was tomorrow, fourth period, twenty-two freshmen in Mr. Mendoza's homeroom, and Mr. Mendoza had said, with that flat certainty of his, "You volunteered, Samuel. The peer health program needs someone, and you're the someone." Samuel had not exactly volunteered. He had raised his hand halfway during a discussion about the school's dismal health curriculum, and Mr. Mendoza had interpreted the gesture the way he interpreted everything, generously and in his own favor, a kind of hermeneutics that always ended with you doing more than you meant to.

Kevin arrived first, letting himself in through the back door as he had since they were nine. "You actually made flashcards," he said, picking one up. "Explain consent. Okay, go. Explain it to me like I'm fourteen and terrified."

"It's not terrified. They're just kids who don't know anything." Samuel took the card back. "Consent means yes, freely, without pressure, and it can be taken back. That's the whole thing. You don't talk someone into it, and silence isn't a yes."

"That's decent. What about the rest?" Kevin flipped through the stack and stopped at the pharmacy receipt Samuel had wedged between two cards. "What's this?"

Samuel had gone to the pharmacy on Tuesday after his shift, ostensibly for his mother's antacids, mostly because the clinic question on his outline had been the one thing he couldn't answer from memory. He wanted to say the words out loud to someone who actually knew. While he waited, a girl from the grade below stood at the counter, holding a paper bag with a birth control prescription in it, and asked the pharmacist, quietly but not shamefully, whether it also protected against infections. Samuel had leaned slightly closer to the vitamin display, feeling like a spy and a student at once. The pharmacist said no, it prevented pregnancy, not infections. She asked what did. "Condoms," the pharmacist said. "They're the only common contraceptive that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections." The girl had nodded, thanked her, and bought a box on the spot, and Samuel had written the sentence in his phone in the parking lot, word for word, because it felt like something you should not paraphrase.

"Flashback," Kevin said when Samuel finished telling it, pointing at him with a fork he'd taken from the drawer without asking. "Very cinematic. But did you buy the antacids?"

"My mom has a penurious relationship with name brands, so yes, the cheap ones." Samuel slid the receipt into his outline. "The point is I had it wrong in my notes. I had 'contraception and STI protection' as one heading like they're the same thing. That's the mistake the whole curriculum makes, honestly. The pill stops pregnancy. It does nothing about infections. If I stand up there tomorrow and blur that together, some kid walks out thinking they're covered when they're not."

Meghan knocked at the front door and came through to the kitchen carrying her own binder, because Meghan never arrived anywhere without supplies. She sat down, read Samuel's outline for ninety silent seconds, then looked up. "You have the condom line in the contraception section. Move it. It needs to be in both, or said twice, because fourteen-year-olds don't carry ideas across sections. They hear the word that applies to them and stop listening."

"That's repetitive."

"Repetition is the entire technology of public health," Meghan said. "Ask any dentist."

Samuel resisted this for about a minute, arranging and rearranging the cards, and then he thought about the girl at the pharmacy counter, how direct the pharmacist had been, how the plainness of the sentence was what made it usable, and he pulled the condom card out and duplicated it in his own handwriting, one for each section. Meghan watched him do it without gloating, which was her way of gloating.

"The testing part is thinner," Kevin said, tapping the last card. "Where do they even go?"

"There's a clinic two bus stops from school. Walk-ins on Thursdays, or you can book ahead, and it's confidential, meaning they don't call your parents even if you're under eighteen." Samuel had called the clinic himself on Wednesday, had asked the receptionist the questions he imagined a freshman would be too embarrassed to ask, and had written down the answers on the back of a water bill. "I'm going to end with that. Not with a warning. With a door they can actually walk through."

Meghan closed her binder. "You changed the whole shape of it since Tuesday," she said. "It's better. It was more polished before, but it didn't know anything."

Samuel looked at the cards, the duplicated line, the water bill, the pharmacy receipt, and understood that polish had never been the problem. He had been trying to burnish an outline when what he needed was to be accurate and plain, and he could not yet say which of the remaining sentences would survive contact with twenty-two freshmen and which would dissolve the moment someone in the back row asked a question he hadn't rehearsed. "Run it with me once," he said. "The whole thing, start to finish, and interrupt me everywhere it's confusing."

Kevin dragged a chair to the end of the table, folded his arms in an impression of a bored fourteen-year-old, and said, "Okay, teach. Convince me why I shouldn't just trust my girlfriend when she says she's on the pill."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
story:
The cuff hissed and tightened around her father's arm until his fingers looked swollen, then let go all at once, and the screen printed 148 over 92. Sienna copied the numbers onto the back of a grocery receipt before they vanished. Her father was watching the television with the sound low, and when she asked what the numbers meant, he shrugged and said the doctor would tell him on Thursday, the way he said things when he didn't want to be an interruption in his own evening.

The monitor had come in a box that still smelled faintly of the pharmacy, along with a booklet she'd never opened because it belonged, she'd assumed, to a milieu of adults with pill organizers and afternoon appointments. She sat on the kitchen floor with it now, cross-legged under the humming refrigerator light, and read. The numbers were pressures, it said, measured in millimeters of mercury. The top number was called systolic, the pressure when the heart beats. The bottom was diastolic, the pressure when the heart relaxes between beats. She read the page twice, mouthing the words, then looked back at the receipt in her hand. 148 when his heart beat. 92 when it rested. Neither of them relaxed.

She remembered, without meaning to, the fall Ms. Wang had kept a chart taped beside the door of the biology room, and the afternoon she'd written her own pulse on it just to see her name in the column beside the athletes'. Jayda had leaned over and said, "You're lower than me. Rude." It had seemed like trivia then, a number belonging to nobody. Now she wondered whether a heart was always saying something like this, every beat, a sentence she'd simply never learned to read.

Her father was still in the living room when she came in with the booklet and the receipt. She knelt beside the couch and showed him the screen's memory, the last three readings lined up like birds on a wire, all of them high in the same quiet way. "The top one's systolic," she said. "That's when the heart beats." She tapped the lower number. "Diastolic is when it relaxes between beats." He looked at the booklet, then at her, and said nothing for a moment, and she understood that he had owned this machine for a month without ever asking what it was telling him, which was its own kind of answer.

"Is that bad?" he asked finally, and she said she thought so, she thought the numbers were supposed to be lower, though the booklet's chart had small print she hadn't finished. What she had finished was the section on changes, the part she'd read three times because it surprised her: diet and exercise, the two things he dismissed as his doctor's hobbyhorses, could move these numbers over months. Not a cure, the booklet was careful to say. A shift. She liked that honesty, the way it refused to promise more than it knew.

"Mary's dad walks at the track every morning," she said. "He started because of this exact thing." Her father grunted, which could have meant anything. She knew his cooking, the Sunday sauce that took half a day and most of a salt box, his epicurean conviction that food worth eating was food that had been seasoned within an inch of its life. She wasn't going to win an argument against that in one evening, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she might not win it at all. What she could do was make the numbers visible to him, make them into something other than Thursday's problem.

She made them a chart instead. On graph paper, in the good pen, she drew two columns and headed them with the two words, and she wrote tonight's reading at the top and left the rows below empty, twenty of them, enough for weeks. She carried it back to the living room and set it on his knee without a speech. "You do it in the morning," she said. "Same chair, before coffee. I'll do the writing."

He looked at the empty rows for a long time, his thumb moving along the edge of the paper as though testing whether it would desiccate and crumble if he touched it too hard. Then he said, "Before coffee," as if testing the shape of a promise, and Sienna got up to put the booklet back in its box, leaving it on the counter where he'd see it in the morning instead of in the drawer where he kept things he meant to forget.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
Aiden had written his grandfather's numbers on his hand before the bus left, and by the time the counselor called his cabin to breakfast the ink had sweated into something barely legible: 134 over 85. He sat at the long table in the lodge at Camp Wren, moving scrambled eggs around his plate, while Jayden across from him argued with Dhruv about whether the lake water was cold enough to count as dangerous.

The health sciences track was Mr. Shin's idea, or rather Mr. Shin's assignment. On the first day of the session he had set a cuff, a stethoscope, and a home monitor log on the picnic table behind the infirmary and said only that by Friday each of them should be able to take a reading, say what it meant, and explain what a person could do about it. Aiden had thought it would be easy. He had watched his grandfather press his thumb into the cuff's button a hundred times on the porch in June, the machine beeping, the little numbers assembling themselves in the window, and he had never once asked what they were.

Now, at breakfast, he kept looking at his hand. Before he'd left for camp, he'd gone through the porch drawer for a phone charger and found the log his grandfather kept, dated in his small square handwriting, two readings a day for most of a month. Nearly all of them sat between 130 and 139 on the top number. Aiden had memorized one and thought, vaguely, that memorizing was the same as understanding.

After breakfast Mr. Shin split them into pairs. Aiden got Dhruv, which meant the blood pressure station, because Dhruv had already declared the bandaging station "an affectation, honestly, gauze and theatrical blood," and strolled toward the cuff with an insouciance that Aiden found enviable and slightly annoying. Dhruv sat, rolled up his sleeve, and grinned.

"Go on. I'm your patient."

Aiden wrapped the cuff the way the diagram showed, tucked the stethoscope under the edge, and squeezed the bulb until Dhruv, who was not actually a good patient and kept talking, complained that his arm was going to fall off. The needle dropped. He watched it, listened, lost the sound, found it. 118 over 74. Dhruv looked pleased with himself, as if he had personally arranged the result.

Mr. Shin came around the table and put a laminated sheet between them. Aiden read it twice. Under the 2017 American guideline, the sheet said, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139, or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89. He said the words to himself. Systolic. The top number. He looked at his own hand again, at the smudged 134 over 85, and something in his stomach shifted.

"Say what you'd tell the person," Mr. Shin said. He was looking at the lake, not at them, which Aiden had learned was how Mr. Shin listened hardest.

Dhruv, being Dhruv, tried first. "I'd say, congratulations, you have stage 1 hypertension, please enjoy your day." Mr. Shin said nothing. The silence did its work, the way it always did with Dhruv, burnishing away the joke until only the actual question was left.

Aiden thought about the porch in June. He thought about his grandfather salting the tomatoes from the garden before he'd even tasted them, and about the summer before that, when the two of them had walked the rail trail every evening and his grandfather had called it their constitutional, an old word that Aiden had adopted as a joke and then quietly kept. The readings from that summer weren't in the log. The log had started this spring, after the walking stopped, after the knee.

"If it were 134 over 85," Aiden said slowly, "that's stage 1 hypertension. Under the 2017 American guideline, that's systolic 130 to 139, or diastolic 80 to 89." He heard his own voice do it, the fact arriving whole out of him, and it didn't feel like showing off. It felt like holding something carefully.

"And then?" Mr. Shin said.

"And then diet and exercise change it, that's the whole point of the assignment. Less salt. Walking again, if the knee could take it, maybe something that doesn't need the knee. But the walking stopped because of the knee, and I don't know if that's why the numbers are where they are, or if it's something else, or if I'm even the person who should be the one saying it." He stopped. Dhruv was watching him without any joke in his face at all.

Mr. Shin finally turned from the lake. "The assignment was to interpret and explain. It didn't say who you had to explain it to."

That evening Aiden sat on the dock with his phone, the log's numbers in his notebook now, copied out properly, a column of them. His grandfather picked up on the second ring. Behind the voice, the porch wind chime, the television nobody was watching. Aiden looked at the column, at 134 over 85 at the top of it, and asked how the knee was doing.

"Knee's fine," his grandfather said. "Why?"

Aiden turned the notebook to the next blank page and clicked his pen. "There's something I want to read you."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice.
story:
The debate had been going for six minutes before Jordan realized he was losing. Mr. Ionescu had split the seminar table in half, presidential systems against parliamentary, and Jordan had taken the presidential side mostly because Mohamed-Amine had called it first on the other. That was how it always went between them; the positions were arbitrary, the arguments were not.

"Say the prime minister turns out to be terrible," Mohamed-Amine said, leaning over his notes. "In a parliamentary system, his own party can replace him. A vote, a signature, done. With a president, you wait years for the next election, or you try impeachment, which almost never works." He said it flatly, without triumph, which somehow made it worse.

Jordan looked down at the article Mr. Ionescu had photocopied for them, something from a political science journal with a crease down the middle. The words ran together. Behind him, Aubree was tapping her pen against the spine of her notebook in that arrhythmic way she had when she was thinking faster than the discussion. The radiator under the window ticked. Somewhere down the hall a door closed.

He thought of his grandfather, and the thought arrived whole, the way memories do when you're cornered. Two winters ago, at the kitchen table, his grandfather had watched a news segment about a foreign election and said, "Over there they can toss the leader out like a bad tenant. Here we hand him the keys for four years and hope." Jordan had been fifteen and hadn't understood, and his grandfather had shrugged and gone back to his coffee rather than explain. He wasn't a pedagogue, his grandfather; he assumed you would figure things out eventually or you wouldn't. Jordan had resented the shrug at the time. Now he recognized it as a kind of respect.

"But that's the point," Jordan said, and heard his own voice steady, which surprised him. "The fixed term is a feature. The voters know exactly how long they've hired someone for. Nobody in a back room can undo their choice. In a parliamentary system, the head of government can fall because of some coalition squabble the voters never voted on." He was building this as he spoke, and he could feel the two ideas grinding against each other like misaligned gears. He believed both halves. That was the problem, and also, he suspected, the beginning of an answer.

Aubree stopped tapping her pen. "Okay, but here's what I never got," she said. "If the fixed term is such a feature, and if the people love a president, why can't he just keep running? Ever. What's the argument there?" She turned her hands over, palms up. Mr. Ionescu, who had been standing by the whiteboard with his arms folded, said nothing and wrote nothing, which Jordan had learned was his way of handing the question to the room.

Jordan opened his notebook and flipped back two pages, to Monday, when they had done the constitutional amendments. There it was, underlined twice in his own handwriting, a fact he had copied and then ignored because it hadn't seemed to matter: the 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in 1951, limits a person to being elected president twice. He read it twice, silently, while Aubree waited and Mohamed-Amine watched him read.

"The 22nd Amendment," Jordan said. "Ratified in 1951. It limits a person to being elected president twice." He let that sit, then kept going because the next part was forming faster than he could second-guess it. "So even a popular president, someone the majority would happily re-elect, is out after two terms. Which means the system doesn't fully trust popularity either. It trusts the calendar." He paused, aware he was about to concede something. "So maybe the parliamentary side is right that removal should be easier, and my side is right that elections should mean something fixed. It's not a contradiction. It's two different bets about which danger you fear more: a leader you can't get rid of, or a majority you can't slow down."

Mohamed-Amine tilted his chair back on two legs, considering. "That's a real position," he admitted. "It's also a fence." The class laughed, and Jordan laughed too, because it was fair. He could introspect all he wanted about which system he'd choose if he were designing a country from scratch, and the honest answer was that he didn't know yet, that the answer felt ductile in his hands, still shapeable, and maybe it was supposed to stay that way a while longer. Mr. Ionescu uncapped a marker and wrote a single word on the whiteboard, then a question mark after it: "Trade-offs?"

Aubree leaned across the aisle and tapped Jordan's notebook, right on the underlined amendment. "Twice," she said. "So what happens the second a president's been elected twice and half the country still wants him?" Jordan closed the notebook and slid it toward the middle of the table, between the two halves, where either side could reach it.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The quiz came back with a red circle around question four, and Jessica had been staring at it since the bell. Mr. Hughes had written "see me" in the margin, which she suspected was his polite way of saying she had no idea what she was doing. Across the lab bench, Tayden was stacking pipette tips into a tower and knocking them over with one finger, quietly, like a bored clockmaker.

"You wrote T," Tayden said, leaning over her paper without asking. "In the RNA. It's not wrong exactly, it's very wrong."

"I know it's wrong. I don't know why it's wrong." Jessica flattened the page against the black counter, next to the sink that never drained properly. Question four gave a strand of DNA and asked for the mRNA it would produce. She had copied it letter for letter, patient as a monk, and every line was poisoned in the same way. A with T, G with C, and where the DNA had an A, she had matched it with another T, as though the rules never changed.

"Come on," Tayden said, and carried her binder over to the window bench where Kristian sat with his hood up, pretending to review for the unit test on Friday. Kristian was the kind of person who read the textbook chapter twice and then complained that it was shallow, so nobody asked him for help unless they were desperate. Jessica was desperate, but she also had her pride, and the two feelings sat together awkwardly on the walk over.

Kristian turned her binder sideways, then right side up again. "You transcribed like it was still DNA," he said. "In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. But this is RNA you're making."

"So what pairs with adenine in RNA?"

"Uracil," he said, and slid a pen across the table to her. She took a clean sheet and wrote it at the top, U for adenine, C for guanine, the way Tayden had once written her locker combination on her hand so she couldn't lose it. Then she worked the sequence again, slowly, and the letters came out different this time, and something small and satisfying clicked into place, like a door that had been unlocked the whole time.

"It's like the cell has two languages," she said. "The same letters, almost, but one of them swapped out. And then translation is a third language, on top of that."

Kristian made a face. "It's not really a language. There's no logos in it, no meaning, it's just chemistry." Tayden said that was the most facetious thing anyone had said all week, since Kristian was the one always going on about information theory at lunch, and for a minute the two of them argued about whether a code could carry meaning without anyone intending it, while Jessica kept writing. She was not sure who was right. It seemed possible that the copying was mindless and that the protein was still, in some real sense, a message, and she did not know how to hold both of those at once except by admitting she held both.

At the end of the period Mr. Hughes stopped her at the door. "Better," he said, looking at her redone sheet. "You'll want to indemnify yourself for Friday, though. One wrong letter and the whole amino acid chain shifts." He meant, she gathered, that she should guard against her own mistakes, check her work, build in some insurance. She said she would, and mostly meant it, and walked out into the hallway holding the sheet with the U at the top of it like a talisman.

On Friday she got the test back with a 94 at the top, circled twice, and she was still smiling at it when she noticed the last question, the extra credit, marked wrong. The prompt asked for the DNA template that would produce a given mRNA strand, and she had paired every adenine in the RNA with a uracil in the DNA, careful and consistent all the way down. Kristian leaned over from the next row and read her answer upside down.

"You put U in DNA," he said. "There's no uracil in DNA. It's thymine."

Jessica looked at her neat, confident letters, every one of them wrong in the same direction, and started laughing before she could stop herself. "So it goes both ways," she said, and copied the correction into her notes.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
Mya had booked the empty room on the tournament schedule three weeks in advance, which meant she had claimed it by taping a torn program to the door with the words ONE-ACT REHEARSAL, 12:30 written in marker that was dying even then. She was signed into the debate itself, Lincoln-Douglas, resolution about wealth distribution, and she had a round at two. Her mother had called debate her annuity, the thing that paid out scholarships year after year, and Mya had not argued, because arguing was the point. But the one-act was hers in a way the resolution wasn't, and so she had learned to compartmentalize: negatives in one pocket, blocking notes in the other, neither allowed to bleed.

Kristopher and Sydnee arrived still wearing their name tags, Sydnee carrying half a sandwich she refused to put down even in character. The play was nine minutes long, two characters, one bench. Mya stood on a chair to see it the way an audience would, which was a thing she'd read in a book about directing and which made her feel faintly ridiculous and faintly official.

The trouble started immediately, and it was the same trouble from every rehearsal. Kristopher's character was restless, written restless, and every time he crossed the room, Sydnee ended up behind him. From the chair Mya watched her lead get swallowed: one walk and half the stage was gone, Sydnee's face just a sliver past his shoulder. "You're hiding," Mya said. Sydnee said she could feel it, actually, like standing behind a door.

Mya told Kristopher to cross upstage instead. He was obdurate about it, in the specific way of actors who have decided a movement belongs to them and not to the text. "He crosses because he can't sit still," Kristopher said. "If I go the long way it reads as calm, and he's not calm." Mya wrote calm?? in her notes and then crossed it out, because it wasn't the crossing that was wrong. She'd seen it in her head a hundred times, that walk, and it was right.

She climbed down and stood where the audience would sit, in the doorway, and watched again, and this time she noticed what her eye did. When Kristopher crossed, the whole picture tilted toward him, like a scale, and her eye wanted Sydnee to move the other way, a little shift, just enough to reopen the picture. She thought about debate, about how you distribute weight across a case; you don't abandon an argument when your opponent extends his, you answer it, you rebalance. She had been so sure the two things lived in separate pockets.

"Sydnee, when he crosses, I want you to counter," Mya said. "Shift downstage, two steps, so the two of you balance the stage and the audience keeps both of you in view." Sydnee took a bite of sandwich and did it, and it worked instantly, visibly, in a way that made Mya suspicious of how easy it was. Kristopher crossed, Sydnee countered, and the stage held both of them like a sentence holding two clauses.

They ran it four more times, and on the third Sydnee did it before he'd finished crossing, like she'd stopped thinking of it as a correction and started thinking of it as hers. Between runs Mya's phone buzzed. A message from Ms. Chanthavong, her drama adviser, who was judging a round two floors up: Heard you commandeered a room. Is the bench still invisible when K walks? Mya typed back, solved it, countering, and then, before sending, deleted "solved it" and wrote "they're balancing each other now." She wasn't sure it was solved, exactly. She wasn't sure whether Sydnee's shift should be big or barely there, whether it changed who had the power in the scene, whether a director was supposed to know or supposed to keep asking. She sent it anyway.

At 1:50 she had to go sign in for her round, and she left them running the scene alone with the door propped open. From down the corridor she could hear the rhythm of it, cross, shift, cross, shift, like something being traded back and forth fairly. She checked her flowpad, found her case on wealth distribution, and realized she was already thinking about how to open her first speech, not with her strongest point stacked on the left, but with two, balanced, both visible at once. Behind her, faintly, Sydnee's voice carried into the hallway: "Do it again. Slower this time."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: If a Java class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one; once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added.
story:
Jaxon had been telling people all week that his BankAccount program was basically finished, which was true only if "basically" carried most of the weight. What he had was a class with private fields and getter methods, and a test file that had run green once, back before he got ambitious. Now he sat cross-legged on the carpet of Gibson's basement, laptop balanced on a chemistry binder, the glow of the screen the brightest thing in a room lit by one dying bulb and a lamp shaped like a guitar.

"The fields have to be private," Keiran said from the couch, where he was folded into a posture that suggested his spine had given up negotiating. "That's the whole maxim of the unit. Encapsulation or whatever. Ms. Ricci says it on every slide."

"I did that part," Jaxon said. "Balance is private. Owner is private. I wrote getBalance and getOwner, they return the values, it's clean." He turned the laptop so they could see. "Watch. I'm going to make it good."

Gibson, who had contributed nothing but the basement and a bag of nacho chips, leaned over anyway. "Make it good how?"

"Right now you can only make an account with nothing in it. Zero dollars. So I'm adding a constructor where you pass in the owner's name and the starting balance." Jaxon typed while he talked, because that was how he did everything, including arguments. "Two parameters. Then my test can set up an account that actually has money."

"That's real progress," Keiran said. "My program is moribund. It has one field and it's misspelled."

Jaxon wrote the constructor, saved, and ran the old test. The console filled with red. He stared at it for a second, the specific blank stare of a person watching something they built quietly stop working.

"No, hold on," he said. "It says it can't find the constructor. The no-argument one. But I never wrote a no-argument one, so what is it even looking for?"

Keiran unwound one arm from the couch. "Show me." He read the error out loud, slowly, like it was a riddle. "Before you added yours, the test made an account with empty parentheses and it worked. You never wrote anything for that."

Jaxon scrolled up through his own history, and the shape of it landed in his stomach before he could have explained it. "So it worked before because the compiler was filling one in," he said. "A default one. And it only does that if you haven't written any constructor yourself. The second I added one with parameters, the free one stopped existing, and the old test is still calling it." He said it out loud twice, testing it against the error on the screen, and it fit everywhere he checked.

"So fix it," Gibson said, mouth full.

"It's not that simple," Jaxon said, and immediately heard how that sounded. "I mean, it is simple to fix, but I have to pick. I can write my own no-argument constructor and keep both, or I can change the test so everything uses the parameters. One of them is easier. The other one is probably what the assignment actually wants."

The phone buzzed against the binder. It was a message from Ms. Ricci, sent to the whole class, and Keiran read it over Jaxon's shoulder: "Reminder for tomorrow's submission: your test file should exercise the constructor you designed, not the empty one. If your old tests broke after you added a constructor, that is worth understanding, not worth deleting."

Jaxon read it twice. "She's talking about exactly this. Exactly, specifically this." He felt caught between embarrassment and something warmer, the feeling of being handed a clue by someone who knew he'd need it. "Okay. So I keep my parameter constructor and I rewrite the test to use it. But then I don't get to pretend the easy way and the right way are the same thing."

"They never were," Keiran said.

"You're so wise," Gibson said. "Write it down and I'll frame it."

"It's not wisdom, it's a maxim," Keiran said. "There's a difference. Wisdom you have to earn."

Jaxon rewrote the test.
