Where it had created an empty account and then, in a clumsy move he wasn't proud of, tried to interpolate a balance by calling a setter that didn't exist, he now built the account with a name and an amount in one line. He added a second test that checked the getters returned exactly what went in. He ran it. Green. He ran it again, because one green run felt like luck and two felt like evidence.

"Nice," Gibson said, and turned the lamp shaped like a guitar toward the screen as if congratulating it. Jaxon closed the laptop halfway, then opened it again to make sure the green was still there.

"Is the bulb up there actually dying, or does it just look like that?" he asked.

"It's been dying since March," Gibson said. "We keep meaning to replace it."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
Anna arrived at the community garden at eight, ten minutes early, because that was what the signup sheet had said and because she wanted the hour to go well. The food bank shared the garden's lot, a squat shed with a loading dock behind the tomato rows, and a hand-lettered sign on the door read, in someone's careful capitals, EVERYTHING COLD GOES IN FIRST. She had come because her school required service hours, which she knew was not the same as wanting to come, and she was still deciding which it was.

A woman named Ms. Leblanc handed her a clipboard and a hairnet and pointed at the dock, where a volunteer named Connor was hauling boxes off a van. "You two sort the dairy," Ms. Leblanc said, and then she was gone toward the garden, where an argument seemed to be brewing over the compost bins. Connor turned out to be from her chemistry class, recognizable only without the lab goggles. He waved with a gallon of milk in each hand.

The milk was wrong. Anna understood this before she could say why: the cartons were sweating, the dock was already warm in the morning sun, and the stack had been sitting apart from the crates of canned goods, closer to the wall, as if someone had set it down and intended to come back. She peeled a thermometer strip off the shelf inside the shed door and pressed it against a carton, the way she had seen Ms. Leblanc do to the cooler an hour earlier, and the strip read eleven degrees. She did not know what that meant until she found the laminated card taped above the cooler, a food-safety card with a highlighted line.

"Refrigerated food has to stay at or below four degrees Celsius," she read aloud, half to herself. "Forty Fahrenheit. To slow bacteria." Connor came in with the last of the stack and looked at the carton in her hand, and then at the strip, and did not say anything for a moment too long.

"It's only been out since I got distracted," he said finally. "There was a wasp."

"How long?" Anna asked. She was not trying to corner him; she genuinely needed to know, because the card did not tell her what happened after the temperature rose, only what the rule was, and the gap between the rule and this sweating carton was suddenly the whole morning. Connor shrugged and said twenty minutes, maybe thirty, and she wrote that down because writing it down felt like doing something.

They carried the stack to Ms. Leblanc, who was still at the compost bins with an older volunteer, and Anna held out the thermometer strip and the clipboard like evidence. Ms. Leblanc looked at the milk, then at Connor, then at the dock, and Anna realized she was deciding something, and that whatever she decided would teach Anna more than the card had.

While Ms. Leblanc checked each carton herself, pressing fresh strips to the plastic, Anna's phone buzzed in her apron pocket. It was a message from George, who volunteered on Saturdays and had signed her up for this shift in the first place. "heads up," it read, "connor got put on probation last month for leaving the eggs out overnight. they almost didn't let him back. he didn't tell ms leblanc he was on the dock alone today. i'm telling you because someone should know and it shouldn't come from me in front of everyone." Anna read it twice. The cartons were going back into the cooler, the ones that still read cold enough, and Ms. Leblanc was marking the rest with a grease pencil, and Connor was standing with his hands in his pockets watching the tomatoes as though they required supervision.

Here was the part Anna had not expected: that the milk was the simple problem and Connor was the hard one. She thought about how Ms. Leblanc had not asked him anything yet, how the question was gathering itself, how George's message adumbrated a history that Anna could only see the edges of, and how the rules on the card gave her nothing for this. She believed in the rules; four degrees was four degrees, and bacteria did not care about intentions. But Connor's face had gone the particular stillness of someone waiting to be found out, and she remembered her own first hour here, when she had nearly mislabeled the bread bin and Connor had fixed it without comment, an idiosyncrasy of his, that quiet fixing, which she now suspected was a kind of apology he kept making.

She stepped over to him while Ms. Leblanc was still at the cooler. "You should tell her before the grease pencil comes out," Anna said quietly. "The wasp part's true, right? Then it's true and it's yours to say." Connor looked at the marked cartons, the incipient pile of discards growing beside them, and Anna understood that she did not know if she was helping him or protecting the food bank from him, and that both might be the same act. He crossed the lot toward Ms. Leblanc, wiping his palms on his jeans, and Anna watched him say the first words she could not hear.

"Start a fresh log line," Ms. Leblanc called back over her shoulder, holding out the grease pencil. "Time, temp, and what we threw out."

Anna took the pencil.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: CIRCLE, a research center at Tufts University, estimated that 50 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 voted in the 2020 presidential election.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard read 2:41, and the voter registration table in the back of Ms. Ramírez's classroom closed at three. Morgan had been carrying the form in her backpack for nine days, folded once, then refolded the other way so the creases crossed like a small argument.

"You're actually doing this," Kian said, sliding into the desk beside hers. He nodded at the form as if it were something she'd shoplifted. "Half of us don't even show up. Salma was reading this thing from CIRCLE, that research center at Tufts. They estimated fifty percent of Americans aged eighteen to twenty-nine voted in the 2020 presidential election. Fifty. A coin flip."

"So the other fifty percent are smart," said a boy near the window, and a few people laughed, the careless laugh that means nobody really thinks it's funny.

Salma turned around in her seat, her braids catching the fluorescent light. "Or the other fifty percent are tired, or working two jobs, or think it doesn't count. That's the point. You can't build a hegemony on fifty percent participation." She said the word the way she said most words, like she'd paid for it and intended to get her money's worth. "The people who benefit from low turnout know exactly what they're doing."

Kian rolled his eyes. "Here it comes."

"I'm not lecturing. I'm saying Morgan's form is a small act against that. One more young person who shows up."

Morgan smoothed the paper flat against her desk. She had spent the drive to school composing the sentence she would say at the table, and now the sentence had dissolved. "It's not that simple," she said, which was true and also a way of saying nothing.

Ms. Ramírez, watering the spider plant by the file cabinet as though she weren't listening, spoke without turning around. "The table closes in fifteen minutes. The county office stops taking forms at three, and tomorrow it's too late for this election." She set the watering can down. "Forms are legal documents. Read what you sign."

At 2:47 Morgan stood in the short line, and it was here, under the putative supervision of two seniors with clipboards who were clearly also guessing at most of the answers, that she actually read the form for the first time. Line 3 asked for date of birth. Line 4 asked whether she would be eighteen on or before election day. Her pen hovered. She did the arithmetic she had been avoiding all week, the arithmetic that was the real reason the form had stayed folded in her backpack.

Her birthday was October thirtieth. Election day was November fifth. Registration closed today, September twenty-seventh, when she was still seventeen.

"Next," said the senior with the clipboard.

"Quick question," Morgan said. Her mouth was dry in the specific way it went dry before a race. "If I'm seventeen now but I turn eighteen before election day. Is that allowed, or..."

The senior looked at the form, then at her, then flipped a laminated sheet over and read it silently, lips moving. Behind Morgan, Kian had appeared in the line with no form of his own, hands in his pockets, watching.

"State law says you can register if you'll be eighteen by election day," the senior said at last. "It's right here. You just check this box."

Morgan checked the box. Her signature came out smaller than she expected, cramped, like something that had been waiting a long time to be needed. The senior stamped the form and dropped it in the envelope, and that was it; no bell, no ceremony, the envelope just sat there already ordinary.

"So it counts," Kian said as they walked out behind Salma. "You're in the fifty percent. The, what do you call it, the good half."

"It's not halves," Morgan said. "It never was." She stopped at the drinking fountain, because she wanted an excuse not to look at either of them. "Salma thinks showing up is how you resuscitate the whole thing. You think staying home is a kind of veto. I think both of you are describing something real, and I only get one line on one form." She drank, wiped her mouth with her sleeve. "Ask me in November."

"It's going to be close," Salma said quietly, looking down the hallway toward the gym, where someone had already begun taping up campaign signs. "Every single one."

"Then I'll be one," Morgan said, and pulled her backpack strap tight on her shoulder.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
The community art studio smelled of turpentine and old radiator dust, and on the first Tuesday of the portfolio program Ms. Addo taped a strip of paper above the sinks that read: TEN WORKS, ONE THEME, ONE STATEMENT. Andrew had signed up because his mother had found the flyer at the library and because he wanted, quietly, something that was his. He sat near the window with Calvin and Sonny, who had both come with sketchbooks already bulging, while Andrew's folder held three drawings of his grandfather's hands and nothing else.

"Hands," Sonny said, looking over. "That's a theme. You could do ten of those."

"It's not a theme," Andrew said. "It's a subject. I don't know what it's about yet."

Ms. Addo, arranging stools, said that this was the most promising sentence she'd heard all evening. Calvin groaned. Sonny laughed. Andrew wrote it in his notebook anyway, unsure whether he'd been complimented or caught.

By the fourth week he had six pieces: the hands, a chipped teacup from the kitchen, the bench at the bus stop where his grandfather used to wait. The work was going well enough that he started the statement early, sitting at the long table by the paint cabinets while Calvin struggled with a canvas beside him. Andrew wrote a page and a half describing how "the artist explores memory through domestic objects" and how "the artist chooses a muted palette to suggest the passage of time." He read it aloud once, quietly, to test the rhythm of it. It sounded like the wall labels at the museum, confident and smooth and not entirely his.

Calvin, who had been eavesdropping without shame, said it sounded like the artist had hired a publicist. Andrew told him to get back to his canvas. But the sentence stuck, the way a burr sticks to a sweater, and that night he typed the paragraph again and could not make himself believe a word of it. He had written around himself, as though describing a stranger who happened to occupy his chair.

At the next session Ms. Addo collected drafts. She read Andrew's while he pretended to mix ochre. She put the page down and said, "Write it again. This time say I." She didn't explain further, only moved on to Calvin's draft and told him it was scathing in a way that might work for him but that he should be sure he meant it. But Andrew had caught the shape of it: an artist's statement is written in the first person, by the artist, to explain the ideas, the methods, and the context behind a body of work. He had been doing the opposite of every part of that, and doing it fluently, which was somehow worse.

He stayed after the session while the radiator ticked and the light went thin and blue over the parking lot. Sonny was still there too, framing a photograph of his grandmother's church shoes. "Say I," Andrew said, mostly to himself. "It's my statement. Nobody else can say it."

"That's the whole point," Sonny said. "That's why it's called a statement and not a review. A review is somebody else's job."

Andrew began again on a clean page. "I draw my grandfather's hands because," he wrote, and stopped, because he did not yet know what came after because. He tried three endings. Because he died before I could ask him what they had built. Because my mother still sets his teacup out on Sundays. Because I am afraid of forgetting and equally afraid of only remembering. Each was true, and none of them agreed with the others, and he understood that he would have to choose, or else admit in the statement that he hadn't. He thought of Calvin calling his draft the work of a publicist, a sycophant flattering an artist who didn't exist, and he thought too of a poster he'd seen at school about students whose voices went unheard, how easy it was to disenfranchise yourself, to hand over your own sentence to a smoother ghost. He had done it in his own handwriting.

The studio emptied. Ms. Addo locked the paint cabinet and came back for her coat. He asked her whether a statement could hold two things at once, grief and the fear of forgetting, without choosing. She considered it while she wound her scarf.

"That depends," she said, "on whether the two things are fighting or whether they're the same thing wearing different coats. You'll find out when you try to build the last four pieces. The statement comes after the work, not before."

He nodded and packed his folder, the six drawings and the blank page folded inside. In the parking lot the cold hit his face and he stood a moment by his bike, breathing white into the dark, then took out the pen he still had in his jacket pocket and wrote on the back of his hand, where he would see it in the morning: because I am the only one left who remembers the bench.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In many parliamentary systems, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election.
story:
The kettle had not been used since June, and Felix had to pry the lid off with a spoon before he could fill it. His grandfather's house smelled of old newspaper and the lavender sachets his grandmother used to sew, though she had been gone two years now and the sachets were running out of their power. He spread his comparative government notes across the kitchen table, the one with the wobbly leg, and set his phone face down beside the sugar bowl.

The exam was Monday. Ms. Banerjee had assigned the essay question before the break: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government. Felix had written half a page in October and stalled there, because the half page was really two lists pretending to be an argument, and he knew it.

His grandfather shuffled in at four, turned on the small television on the counter, and stood close to it the way he stood close to everything now. A news channel. A parliament somewhere, a crowded chamber, a division bell, members filing through lobbies to vote. "They're doing something," his grandfather said, mostly to himself, and lowered himself into the chair opposite Felix's papers.

The speaker announced the result, and Felix's grandfather leaned forward. "What does it mean, then, when it fails like that?"

Felix looked at the scroll running along the bottom of the screen and found the words he needed. "It was a vote of no confidence," he said, reading aloud, then setting the phone aside because the rest he had to work out himself. He watched the screen. The prime minister stood, gathered nothing, and the chamber began to empty in a strange, unhurried way, like a theatre after a bad play. Felix turned back to his notes, found the empty second half of the page, and wrote: government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election.

It landed on him slowly, the way the fact reshaped everything around it. Nobody waited for a fixed term. Nobody had to be impeached. The chamber itself could pull the plug, and the whole apparatus of government went with it, or went to the country. He underlined the line twice, then thought of the American system he'd grown up hearing about, where a president could lose the Congress, lose the room, lose half the country, and still sit in the office for years because the term belonged to the office, not to the support.

He texted Phoenix, who was also studying, in his way, which involved a laptop and loud music in a language Felix didn't speak. Did you get the removal part. Phoenix replied eight minutes later: presidential = fixed term, hard to remove, right? and Felix typed back: yes but parliamentary one vote can end it. Then he typed more, then deleted it, because text was where nuance went to die.

Malak called at five. "I'm stuck on choosing," she said. "How the head of government gets picked. Is it the voters?"

"It depends which system," Felix said, and he heard his own voice take on that careful tone he disliked in other people. In a parliamentary system, he said, the party in the lower house chose the prime minister, so voters picked members and the members picked the head of government. In a presidential system the voters chose the president directly, separately, a name on a ballot. "So removing is different too," he went on. "In parliament, lose the lower house's confidence and you're finished, resign or call an election. A president can't be removed that way. The term holds."

There was a pause on the line, the sound of Malak writing. "But which is better?" she asked.

Felix looked at his grandfather, who had fallen asleep in front of the news, the scroll still running its silent loop, the same chamber now empty except for cleaners moving through the green benches. Better. He had two lists, and now he had the fact that joined them, and he still didn't have better. He liked the directness of choosing a president by name. He liked, in a way he couldn't yet defend, that a parliament could end a government in an afternoon, that power stayed conditional, on sufferance. Maybe both instincts were about the same thing, the fear of being stuck with someone, or the fear of never being consulted properly, and the systems just answered the fear differently.

"I don't know yet," he said. "Ask me after the exam."

His grandfather woke when the kettle, forgotten, rattled against the stove. Felix turned it off, poured the water over the last of his grandmother's tea, and brought the cup to the table. His grandfather wrapped both hands around it and studied the scattered notes. "That vote," he said. "So the government is out?"

"Resigns, or they call a general election." Felix squared the pages against the table edge. "It's not like here. It can just be over."

His grandfather sipped his tea and watched the empty chamber on the screen, where a woman with a clipboard was counting something along the third row. "Huh," he said.

Felix sat back down and uncapped his pen. The second half of the page was still blank, but it was blank the way a field is before planting, and outside the kitchen window the light was going the particular blue of early winter. He wrote the first sentence of the new draft: In a parliamentary system, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election; in a presidential system, nothing in the legislature can do this. He read it over, and crossed out nothing.

"Grandpa," he said, "is the tea still good?"

His grandfather held the cup up to the window, tilting it against the last of the light.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
Naomi set the table the way her mother liked, forks tines up, because Noor was coming for dinner and her mother believed that company meant ceremony. Noor arrived with garlic bread wrapped in foil and her duffel bag over one shoulder, straight from practice, hair still wet at the temples. They had a regional semifinal in nine days, and Noor, who played setter better than anyone Naomi had ever seen, had spent the whole season serving into the net.

At dinner the talk went everywhere, the way it always did when Noor was there. She was garrulous in the best sense, filling the room with stories about the biology teacher's aquarium disaster and her little brother's campaign to be class treasurer. Naomi's mother kept refilling her plate. It was easy, sitting there, to let the semifinal drift to the edge of the evening, and that was exactly what Naomi had told herself she would not do. Last year Reet had done it. Reet had watched their relay teammate flub exchanges all season and said nothing, week after week, because the teammate was sensitive and Reet was kind, and they had lost the final by two points. Reet had cried on the bus afterward and said, "I thought I was being a good friend." Naomi had thought about that sentence for a year.

She had also thought about a book. Reet's older sister had left it on the kitchen counter over the summer, and Naomi had read it in three nights. When she'd told Reet the title, Reet had shrugged and said, "Radical Candor, yeah," as if the words themselves were the whole argument. But Naomi had underlined one page: in her 2017 book, Kim Scott argued that good feedback combined caring personally about someone with challenging them directly. Neither half worked alone. Naomi had tested this in small ways, once telling a freshman her footwork was late and her spike would be terrifying once she fixed it, and the freshman had fixed it. Still, a freshman was not Noor. Noor was her best friend on the team, and the serving statistic sat between them like a fourth chair at the table.

Her mother cleared the plates and went to the kitchen, which Naomi suspected was not an accident. Mothers were strategic in ways they never admitted.

"I have to say something," Naomi said, "and I need you to let me finish."

Noor put down her fork. "Okay."

"Your serve. It's been off since March, and nobody's told you, and I've been part of the nobody." She had rehearsed this in the shower that morning, stripped of every hedge, and it came out faster than she'd planned. "You're tossing too far back. Coach said it once in February and never followed up. And you're the best setter in the region, so everyone assumes you'll fix it yourself, but you haven't, because nobody's told you it's a problem worth fixing."

Noor was quiet long enough that Naomi could hear the water running in the kitchen.

"Too far back," Noor said finally.

"Your toss. You let it drift behind your head and then you have to reach for it."

"I know," Noor said. "I can feel it. I thought if I hit it harder it would carry anyway." She looked at her hands. "Why didn't you say something in March?"

The question deserved a real answer, and Naomi gave her one. "Because you're my friend and I didn't want to be the one making you feel bad. Which is stupid, because if we lose on Thursday because of it, I'll feel worse." She had worked out her position over many nights, holding Reet's silence in one hand and the book's injunction in the other, and she still wasn't certain where kindness ended and cowardice began. She said so. "I don't think being harsh is honest. I think being specific is honest. There's a difference and I'm still figuring out what it is."

Noor picked up the foil-wrapped bread, then set it down again. "Show me the toss thing. After dinner."

"In the driveway?"

"The streetlight's enough."

They finished the dishes together, Noor drying each plate with exaggerated care, and then went out in their socks with the one ball Naomi kept by the door. Under the orange light Noor served four balls short, then adjusted something in her wrist, some small internal correction, and the fifth one cleared the basketball hoop and hit the neighbour's fence with a clean, deep sound. She served ten more like that. On the last one she turned to Naomi, breathing hard, and said, "You're going to have to do this to me again sometime."

"Probably Thursday," Naomi said, and bounced her the ball.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The line at the bank on Wednesday afternoon moved slowly enough that Landon had read both leases twice before he reached the teller. He was there to convert the cash from his graduation cards into a deposit, and he had brought the leases because his mother had said, over breakfast, that if he was going to sign anything he should at least know what he was signing. One lease was for a room in Leon's cousin's basement, five hundred a month, utilities included, one year fixed. The other was a two-bedroom flat Lewis wanted to share, nine hundred split two ways, plus hydro and internet, also one year fixed.

The teller counted his bills without looking at the papers spread on the counter beside his elbow. When she slid the receipt across, Landon gathered the leases and carried them to the row of chairs by the window, where an old man in a grey cardigan was waiting for an appointment with someone at the desk marked Mr. Wilson. The man glanced at the pages.

"Renting?" he said.

"Trying to figure out which one's actually cheaper," Landon said. "The one with utilities included looks more expensive but maybe isn't."

"That's arithmetic," the man said. "Sit down, then. I've got twenty minutes and nothing to do with them."

Landon sat. He had a pen and the back of a hydro bill he'd found at home, and he worked the numbers while the man watched. The basement room came to five hundred flat. The flat with Lewis came to four hundred fifty for rent, but hydro in an old building with electric heat could run a hundred and change in winter, and internet was sixty split two ways, so call it five forty, sometimes more, sometimes less. He wrote both totals and underlined them.

"Your problem isn't the arithmetic," the man said. "Your problem is the one year."

Landon said his mother had said the same thing, though not why. The man said he wasn't going to explain it either, that Landon's grandfather probably could, and that a boy about to sign a contract should phone his grandfather before he signed anything. Then a woman in a bank uniform called his name, "Mr. Wilson will see you now," and the man stood, buttoned his cardigan, and left Landon alone with the chairs and the underlined numbers.

He went outside and called from the bench by the bike racks. His grandfather picked up on the fourth ring, background noise of a kettle.

"Landon. You got my card?"

"I got it. Thanks. I'm signing a lease, maybe. Both of them are fixed-term, one year, and I don't know if I'll still be in this city next year, and the landlord on the flat keeps saying we have to commit."

"Commit," his grandfather repeated, in the tone he used for words he found suspicious. "Listen. In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms."

Landon wrote this on the hydro bill under the totals. "So the one year is just the one year."

"That's what I told your uncle when his landlord pushed him for a new lease after his first year. Don't worry, I said. He didn't sign. He stayed anyway, month to month, until he bought the house."

"So it's not a trap."

"It's a trap for people who don't phone their grandfathers," his grandfather said, and Landon laughed, and they talked about the kettle and whether his grandfather should be climbing ladders to clean his gutters, which Landon's mother said he should not.

He walked back toward the bank to get his bike, and Lewis was leaning against the racks scrolling his phone. Lewis asked whether he'd decided. Landon laid the hydro bill on the seat of the bike and showed him the two totals, five hundred flat against five forty and floating, and said the floating one averaged worse in winter because electric heat in an old building could transmute a mild November into a hundred-dollar bill by January.

"Then the basement," Lewis said.

"The basement's a room in Leon's cousin's house. If I hate it, I'm stuck a year."

"You're not, though. That's the thing you just told me. After the year it goes month to month."

"That's if they do it right. If Leon's cousin is the kind of guy who follows the rules."

Lewis picked at the tape on the handlebar. "My cousin's landlord made her sign a new lease every year. She thought she had to."

"Maybe she didn't have to. Maybe nobody told her."

They stood there while a bus went by. Landon looked at his numbers again, the underlined totals, the line from his grandfather beneath them, and understood that he had been comparing two leases as if the comparison were only arithmetic, when the real difference was what happened after the year ended, and that after the year he could not price at all. The basement room was cheaper and certain. The flat cost more and carried Lewis, whom he had known since grade nine and whom he trusted except about dishes, Lewis's one persistent peccadillo being that he left them in the sink until they transmuted, in Landon's private accounting, from dishes into a kind of geological deposit.

The choice felt larger than five hundred versus five forty, though he knew it wasn't, really; it was a room, a year, a city he hadn't started living in yet. He thought about phoning the flat's landlord and asking, straight out, what happens at the end of the term, just to hear whether the man said the true thing or the pushy thing. That would tell him something the numbers didn't.

"I'm going to call the landlord tonight," he said. "Ask him about the end of the lease."

"And if he says you have to sign a new one?"

"Then I'll know what kind of landlord he is," Landon said, folding the hydro bill into his back pocket. "Meet me at the library tomorrow. Bring the hydro bills from your old place, if you can find them."

Lewis said he'd look, and Landon got on his bike and rode home with the two leases zipped into his jacket, the pen still in his hand.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Recipients in an email's Bcc field are hidden from everyone else, which is why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other often use Bcc to protect their addresses.
story:
The volunteer office smelled of instant coffee and old paper, and Justine had habituated to it so completely that she only noticed on Mondays, when the weekend had given her nose a chance to forget. Mr. Ndlovu kept a corkboard of thank-you cards behind his desk, pinned in rows like butterflies, and today he was frowning at his laptop as though it had personally insulted him.

"I have to send the schedule for the reading programme to fifty parents," he said when she hung up her jacket. "But every time I send to a group, they all write back to everyone, and then a man named Gerald replies all with a joke about pigeons, and I get forty emails about pigeons." He rubbed his eyes. "The addresses are all just there, in one long line, everyone seeing everyone."

Justine set down her bag. She had learned the trick in her own inbox months ago, after her mother had sent the family reunion details to twenty relatives with every address showing, and an uncle she'd never met had begun forwarding chain letters to the whole list. She leaned over Mr. Ndlovu's shoulder and pointed at the empty field two rows below "To."

"Put the parents' addresses there," she said. "It's called Bcc. The people in it are hidden from everyone else in the email. That's why messages to a long list of people who don't know each other usually go out that way, to protect their addresses."

Mr. Ndlovu looked at the field, then at her, then back at the field, the way a connoisseur inspects a painting he suspects might be genuine. "Blind carbon copy," he murmured, mostly to himself. "I have been printing labels and hand-delivering schedules for two years."

"Which is why you know every parent by face," Justine said, and he laughed, which she had learned was the best part of Thursdays.

He drafted the message right there, typing with two fingers while she unpacked the book crates for Saturday's session. The draft was warm and apologetic and, by the third paragraph, slightly chaotic: an opening that said "Dear friends," a schedule buried in the middle, and a closing that asked parents to "please, if possible, kindly consider maybe replying." Justine read it when he turned the screen toward her, and she hesitated, because she was seventeen and he ran this office and it wasn't her place to say it was a mess.

"You could put the schedule in a table at the top," she said carefully. "So people find it before the greeting even finishes. And maybe one clear sentence at the end about replying, with a deadline."

He was quiet for a moment. "It will feel cold," he said. "These parents, some of them I've known since their children were in nappies. Structure is for lawyers."

"I don't think it has to be either," Justine said, and she pulled the spare chair around and typed a version while he watched. She kept his "Dear friends" and his closing line about Gerald's pigeons being welcome at the sessions, but she front-loaded the table, underlined the reply deadline, and cut everything that repeated anything else. Then she scrolled up so he could see both drafts at once. "Same warmth," she said. "Different order."

Mr. Ndlovu read it twice. When Amine arrived for his shift, ten minutes late and blaming a bus with the belligerent confidence of someone who had not checked the timetable, Mr. Ndlovu was still reading, mouthing certain phrases to himself.

"This table," he said at last. "Gerald will hate it. Gerald thrives on confusion." He moved the cursor to the Bcc field and began pasting addresses, one at a time, checking each name against his paper list. "But the mothers who wrote to me last term saying their inboxes were full of strangers, they will sleep better tonight."

Amine leaned in the doorway with a crate of picture books balanced on his hip. "Why are we all staring at one email?"

"Because it's a good one," Justine said, and meant it, though she wasn't sure whether the goodness lived in the table or the pigeons or the hidden field, or whether those could even be separated. She had come into the office with one idea about how formal things should sound, and she was leaving with something less tidy: that structure and warmth weren't rivals so much as neighbours, and that she would keep testing where the fence between them actually stood.

Mr. Ndlovu hovered his finger over send, then lifted it. "You do it," he said, sliding the laptop toward her. "You built the thing. Bcc list and all."

Justine pressed send, and the three of them watched the screen as the message vanished toward fifty hidden inboxes, Amine still holding the crate, the coffee pot ticking as it cooled.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
The parking lot behind Halstead's Grocery sloped downward toward the delivery entrance, and on Saturday mornings it was empty enough that Mr. Sinclair had begun meeting Samuel there at eight, before the lot filled with carts. Samuel had been driving for seven months on a permit, and the test was on Tuesday, and the only thing left to fail at was parking. He had a green apron folded on the back seat of Mr. Sinclair's sedan because his shift started at ten.

"Tires to the curb," Mr. Sinclair said from the passenger seat, sipping coffee from a paper cup he had brought from home. Samuel eased the car into the space between two orange cones Mr. Sinclair had set up against the curb, reversing until the tires kissed the concrete. It had taken four Saturdays, but the motions had begun to internalize; his hands knew the quarter-turn of the wheel before his mind named it.

Up front, near the automatic doors, Ashlyn was arranging shopping baskets with unusual attention. Samuel had watched her through the windshield all morning. She wanted the Friday closing shift, which paid a dollar more and meant the register counted in your name, and she had asked the manager twice already. Twice refused. Now she was doing the kind of small, visible work that she believed managers noticed, straightening baskets that nobody had messed up.

Edgar pushed a train of carts past the cones and paused. "You're still doing this?" he called. "You parked. It's over. Celebrate."

"He parks facing downhill," Mr. Sinclair said mildly. "Samuel, before you take the key out. Which way do the wheels point?"

Samuel kept his hands on the wheel. He had read the manual twice on his phone in the break room, but reading was not the same as standing in a sloped lot with a curb two feet from his tires. He thought about what would happen if everything else failed, if the brakes gave up on a hill, where the car would want to go. Not into the street where other cars were. Into something that would stop it.

"Toward the curb," he said. "Turn them toward the curb. That way the car rolls into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail." He turned the wheel and cut the engine, and the little sedan sat still against its own front tires.

"Show me the merge next," Mr. Sinclair said. "Then I'll let you go stack whatever it is you stack."

The on-ramp to Route 9 was a quarter mile from the store, and Samuel took it with his blinker on early, glancing at the mirror, matching speed to the flow. A pickup let him in with a small dip of its headlights. It was easier than the parking, easier than the cones, easier than the quiet mathematics of wheels and slopes. On the way back he drove past the store and saw Ashlyn through the glass at a register, counting someone's change, and Edgar in the lot chasing a runaway cart that the wind had made capricious.

After the lesson, Samuel clocked in and found her restocking candy, which was not her section. "You got the register?" he asked.

"For today only." She tore open a box of mints. "If I do it well, maybe Friday. The manager said prove it. So I'm proving it." She said this without bitterness, which surprised him, and he understood that proving it might be its own kind of work, separate from the reward.

He thought about that while bagging groceries, about the difference between knowing something because you had read it and knowing it because your hands had turned the wheel and the car had stayed. Mr. Sinclair had a habit of ending lessons with some small remark he called an epigram, and today's had been, "The road forgives less than the curb does." Samuel was not sure he agreed. The road, in his limited experience, forgave a great deal as long as you signaled. It was the small spaces, the two feet between tire and concrete, that demanded exactness. He could hold both of those ideas at once without deciding between them, which felt like something he was supposed to apologize for and didn't.

At nine that evening, after his shift, he walked out to his mother's old car, the one he would take the test in, and sat in the lot where the light from the store still reached. The lot sloped gently toward the street. He started the engine, pulled into the space beside the cart corral, and turned the front wheels toward the curb, feeling the small resistance as the tire met concrete.

Ashlyn came out with her jacket over her arm and stopped beside his window. He rolled it down.

"Practicing?" she said.

"Proving it," Samuel said, and shut off the engine.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
The library smelled of warm dust and the lemon polish the custodian used on the tables by the window, and Grayson had spread his grandfather's graph paper across two carrels, which was against the unwritten rules but nobody had said anything yet. On the paper, in his grandfather's careful hand, was a parabola, drawn from a table of values, rising from the corner of the page. Under it, in the squares of the grid, his grandfather had shaded the region between the curve and the bottom axis, and in the margin he had written, "How many squares, do you think? Count them."

Grayson had spent Sunday afternoon at the house counting. He had counted the full squares first, then the partial ones, estimating each sliver by eye, and he had come out to something near thirty-three of the hundred small squares his grandfather had ruled off from x equals zero to x equals one. A third, give or take. His grandfather had nodded slowly and said only, "There's a way to know exactly. They'll teach you, or you'll find it."

"Are you actually doing math for fun," Nova said, dropping her bag on the chair across from him. Nyah followed with two cartons of chocolate milk and slid one in front of Grayson like a bribe.

"It's for the test Friday," Grayson said, which was partly true. Mr. Aquino had promised the test would include integrals, a word Grayson had only just learned to say without feeling like he was mispronouncing something in a language he didn't speak. "But also, my grandfather drew this curve, y equals x squared, and asked me to find the area under it, and I counted squares and got about a third, and now there's supposed to be a method that gets it exactly, and it's bothering me that I don't know it."

Nyah leaned over the graph paper. "So the curve is this one," she said, tracing it, "and the area is all this shaded part, from zero to one."

"From x equals zero to x equals one," Grayson said. "That's the part he shaded."

Nova pulled the second carrel over with a screech that made the boy at the microfilm machine look up. She opened Grayson's textbook to the chapter he'd flagged and began reading, faster than he could. Nyah, meanwhile, took out a sheet of her own paper and started drawing rectangles under the parabola, skinny ones, more of them than Grayson had used. "Look," she said, "if you use little rectangles, the tops stick out over the curve. But if you use more and more of them, skinnier and skinnier, the sticking-out part shrinks." She drew another set, thinner still, the staircase of their tops hugging closer to the curve. "It's like the curve is an asymptote the rectangles get closer and closer to but never quite touch. Except somehow, at the end, they do."

"That's it," Nova said quietly, still reading. "That's what the integral is. It's the sum of all the rectangles when they get infinitely skinny." She turned the book so Grayson could see the notation, the long S shape and the numbers zero and one sitting at its base like feet.

Grayson sat with that for a moment. He had been thinking of the area as a thing to count, square by square, the way his grandfather had taught him to count everything, from the change jar to the stars in Orion's belt. Nyah was thinking of it as a limit, a thing approached. He tried to hold both pictures at once: the shaded squares, faithful and approximate, and the rectangles collapsing toward the curve, exact and impossible to draw.

"So what's the answer, then," Nyah said. "For this one. Does the book have this exact curve?"

Grayson searched the examples. He found the function written with the numbers zero and one, ran his finger along the worked line the way Nova indicated, and arrived at a fraction. He checked it twice. One third.

He laughed once, short, and put his hand flat on the graph paper, over the shaded region his grandfather had drawn before the winter. "A third. It's exactly one third. I counted thirty-three squares out of a hundred on Sunday and I thought I was a little off, but I wasn't. I was just measuring the same thing with a cruder ruler."

Mr. Aquino passed behind them on his way to the reference shelf, paused, looked at the graph paper, and looked at Grayson. "Whose curve is that?"

"My grandfather's," Grayson said. "He died in March. This was the last thing he drew for me."

Mr. Aquino was quiet, then said, "That's a perspicacious man, giving you a question instead of an answer." He walked on toward the shelves.

Nova closed the book. "So for Friday, you just do this with other functions? Other curves?"

"Other curves, other numbers at the bottom of the S," Grayson said. "And there's more in the later chapters, ways to parametrize a curve, take a whole different kind of area, and I haven't looked at any of it yet." He folded the graph paper along his grandfather's creases, slid it into his notebook between two pages of notes, and set the chocolate milk aside unopened. He looked at the empty carrel, at the outline of the squares still faintly pressed into the wood.

"Another hour before the library closes," Nyah said, taking out a fresh sheet. "Same curve again, or a new one?"

Grayson uncapped his pen. "Draw me one I've never seen."
